coronary-artery-disease.name: Coronary artery disease
coronary-artery-disease.definition: Narrowing of the coronary arteries by fatty plaque (atherosclerosis), limiting blood flow to the heart muscle.
coronary-artery-disease.overview: Plaque builds up over decades in the arteries that supply the heart. When a narrowing limits flow during exertion the muscle becomes short of oxygen and signals this as angina; when a plaque ruptures and a clot blocks the artery, the result is a heart attack. It is the leading cause of death worldwide, and largely preventable.

structures: Trunk of anterior interventricular branch of left coronary artery
Circumflex branch of left coronary artery
Marginal branch of right coronary artery

causes: Atherosclerosis: cholesterol-rich plaque forming in the artery wall, driven by inflammation
riskFactors: Family history of early heart disease
signs: Often none between attacks
Signs of risk factors: high blood pressure, xanthelasma, nicotine staining
coronary-artery-disease.diagnosis: The story of exertional chest pressure relieved by rest is the key. An ECG may be normal at rest; a stress test, CT coronary angiography or invasive angiography shows the narrowings. Blood tests assess cholesterol, glucose and kidney function.
coronary-artery-disease.treatment: Lifestyle change and medication for everyone: stop smoking, statins to lower LDL, aspirin to prevent clots, blood pressure and diabetes control, and drugs to relieve angina (nitrates, beta blockers). Significant narrowings can be opened with angioplasty and a stent or bypassed with surgery.
coronary-artery-disease.prevention: Not smoking, regular exercise, a diet low in saturated fat and salt, healthy weight, and treating blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.
coronary-artery-disease.seekCare: Call emergency services for chest pain lasting more than a few minutes, or angina that is new, more frequent or occurs at rest.

myocardial-infarction.name: Heart attack (myocardial infarction)
myocardial-infarction.definition: Death of heart muscle because a coronary artery is suddenly blocked, usually by a clot forming on a ruptured plaque.
myocardial-infarction.overview: Every minute of blockage kills more muscle, so a heart attack is treated as a race to reopen the artery. Survival and the amount of muscle saved depend on how quickly the person calls for help and reaches a hospital able to perform emergency angioplasty.

structures: Trunk of anterior interventricular branch of left coronary artery
Posterior interventricular branch of right coronary artery

causes: Rupture of an atherosclerotic plaque with clot formation
Less often: coronary spasm, spontaneous artery dissection, severe anaemia or oxygen lack with a fixed narrowing
riskFactors: Same as coronary artery disease: smoking, cholesterol, blood pressure, diabetes, family history, age
signs: Pale, sweaty, distressed
Fast or slow pulse, low or high blood pressure
Crackles in the lungs if the heart is failing
complications: Rupture of the heart wall or a papillary muscle
myocardial-infarction.diagnosis: An ECG within ten minutes of arrival shows ST elevation (STEMI) when a large artery is fully blocked; troponin in the blood rises over hours and confirms muscle damage in other cases. Echocardiography shows which wall has stopped moving.
myocardial-infarction.treatment: Aspirin immediately, then emergency angioplasty with a stent to reopen the artery (or clot-dissolving drugs if angioplasty is not reachable within about two hours). Afterwards: a second antiplatelet drug, a statin, a beta blocker and an ACE inhibitor, cardiac rehabilitation and risk factor control.
myocardial-infarction.prevention: The measures that prevent coronary artery disease; after a first attack, lifelong medication and rehabilitation halve the risk of another.
myocardial-infarction.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately for crushing chest pain, pain spreading to the arm or jaw, or chest discomfort with sweating, breathlessness or nausea. Do not drive yourself.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.definition: A syndrome in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, or can do so only at raised filling pressures.
heart-failure.overview: Heart failure is the end result of damage from heart attacks, high blood pressure, valve disease or cardiomyopathy. Blood backs up behind the failing ventricle: fluid in the lungs causes breathlessness, fluid in the tissues causes swelling. It is a chronic condition managed with drugs that reduce the heart's workload and, in some cases, devices. Coronary artery disease is the commonest cause, followed by high blood pressure, valve disease and cardiomyopathy; lung disease, congenital heart disease and, rarely, heart tumours also contribute, and obesity, diabetes, smoking, heavy alcohol and cocaine use raise the risk. People notice breathlessness on exertion or at rest, fatigue that worsens with activity, swelling of the feet and ankles that can spread up the legs, and sometimes light-headedness or fainting; some mainly have reduced exercise tolerance, others mainly swelling. There is no cure, but treatment controls symptoms, slows progression and improves quality of life.
causes: Coronary artery disease and previous heart attacks
High blood pressure
Valve disease
Cardiomyopathies (genetic, viral, alcohol, chemotherapy)
Atrial fibrillation
Congenital heart disease
Lung disease
signs: Raised jugular venous pressure
Crackles at the lung bases
Pitting ankle oedema
Enlarged liver
Third heart sound
Weight gain from fluid retention
complications: Acute decompensation triggered by missed medicines or excess salt and fluid
heart-failure.diagnosis: Blood natriuretic peptide (BNP) is raised; echocardiography measures the ejection fraction and finds the cause. ECG, chest X-ray and blood tests for kidney function and anaemia complete the picture. The diagnosis needs both symptoms or signs and objective evidence of heart dysfunction, which is why echocardiography is central: it measures the ejection fraction, separating reduced from preserved ejection fraction, and shows valve disease and the wall-motion abnormalities left by previous infarcts. A 24-hour ECG is used when a rhythm disturbance is suspected, and breathing tests check whether a lung problem is contributing to the breathlessness.
heart-failure.treatment: Diuretics relieve fluid overload; ACE inhibitors or ARNI, beta blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists and SGLT2 inhibitors prolong life in reduced ejection fraction. Salt and fluid moderation, daily weights, vaccination and exercise rehabilitation. Selected patients receive pacemakers, defibrillators or, rarely, transplantation. Treatment depends on the stage. Early on the aim is to prevent progression through risk-factor control and medicines such as statins, beta blockers and renin-angiotensin system inhibitors; later, procedures such as valve repair or an implantable defibrillator are added. Acute deteriorations (decompensation) are often triggered by missed medicines or by exceeding salt and fluid limits, so identifying and treating the trigger is part of each admission, and daily weighing lets fluid gain be caught early. Lifestyle changes, including lower salt intake, run alongside the medicines throughout.
heart-failure.prevention: Treating blood pressure and coronary disease early, limiting alcohol, and controlling diabetes. Because coronary disease causes most heart failure, the measures that prevent heart attacks (not smoking, blood pressure and cholesterol control, physical activity and a healthy weight) prevent most heart failure too.
heart-failure.seekCare: Seek urgent help for breathlessness at rest, waking at night gasping, pink frothy sputum, chest pain, fainting, or rapid weight gain (more than 2 kg in three days).

references.title: British Heart Foundation: Heart failure - causes, symptoms and treatment

atrial-fibrillation.name: Atrial fibrillation
atrial-fibrillation.definition: A common heart rhythm disorder in which the atria quiver chaotically instead of contracting, producing an irregular and often fast pulse.
atrial-fibrillation.overview: In atrial fibrillation the sinoatrial node loses control and hundreds of electrical impulses a minute swirl through the atria; the atrioventricular node lets an irregular selection through. Blood stagnates in the fibrillating left atrium and can clot, which is why AF causes one in five strokes. Many people have no symptoms and the rhythm is found at a routine pulse check or on an ECG done for another reason. When symptoms occur, NHLBI describes fatigue as the commonest, with palpitations felt in the chest, throat or neck, breathlessness on lying down or exercising, chest pain, light-headedness or fainting and low blood pressure. AF is not usually life-threatening in itself, but left untreated it can lead to stroke, heart failure, blood clots, sudden cardiac arrest and cognitive impairment or dementia, which is why detection and treatment matter even when the rhythm is painless.
causes: High blood pressure
Coronary artery disease and heart failure
Valve disease, especially mitral
Overactive thyroid
Alcohol binges
Lung disease and sleep apnoea
Often no single cause in older people
signs: Irregularly irregular pulse
Pulse deficit (heart rate higher than the wrist pulse)
Low blood pressure during a fast episode
complications: Heart failure from a persistently fast rate
atrial-fibrillation.diagnosis: An ECG shows no P waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm. The clinician asks about symptoms, lifestyle, other conditions and any family history of AF. Brief, paroxysmal episodes are caught with a Holter monitor or patch recording over 24 hours or longer, or increasingly with a wearable. Echocardiography looks for valve disease and atrial size; blood tests check thyroid function, kidney function, electrolytes and a blood count, with clotting studies if an anticoagulant is to be started. A chest X-ray is often done to look at the heart and lungs.
atrial-fibrillation.treatment: Treatment has three goals: preventing clots, controlling the heart rate and, where appropriate, restoring normal rhythm. Rate control uses beta blockers, rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers or digoxin. Rhythm control, with electrical cardioversion, antiarrhythmic drugs or catheter ablation, is recommended for people who remain symptomatic or are not improving on rate-controlling medicines; surgical approaches are used in selected cases. Stroke prevention with an anticoagulant such as warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant is offered when the stroke risk score (which weighs age, high blood pressure, heart failure, diabetes and previous clots or stroke) justifies it. Underlying problems such as thyroid disease and sleep apnoea are treated, and lifestyle changes include aiming for a healthy weight and limiting alcohol and stimulants that raise the heart rate.
atrial-fibrillation.prevention: Control blood pressure, weight, alcohol and sleep apnoea; keep active. Treating the conditions that provoke AF, including thyroid disease and sleep apnoea, and limiting alcohol and stimulants reduce the chance of episodes.
atrial-fibrillation.seekCare: Urgent care for palpitations with chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness, and emergency services for any stroke symptoms. NHLBI advises emergency care when palpitations are accompanied by dizziness, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain or fainting.

hypertension.name: High blood pressure (hypertension)
hypertension.definition: Persistently raised arterial pressure, usually defined as 140/90 mmHg or more in the clinic (135/85 on home readings).
hypertension.overview: High blood pressure rarely causes symptoms but silently damages arteries, heart, brain, kidneys and eyes over years. It affects around one adult in three and is the single biggest contributor to stroke and heart disease worldwide. Treatment is cheap and effective, yet half of those affected do not know they have it.
causes: Primary (essential) hypertension in over 90%: genes, salt, weight, alcohol, inactivity, age
Secondary causes in the rest: kidney disease, adrenal tumours, narrowed renal arteries, sleep apnoea, some drugs (NSAIDs, steroids, the pill), pregnancy
signs: Usually none; very high pressure can show retinal changes, an enlarged heart or kidney damage
hypertension.diagnosis: Repeated readings in clinic confirmed by home or 24-hour ambulatory monitoring. Blood and urine tests, an ECG and eye examination look for organ damage and secondary causes.
hypertension.treatment: Lifestyle first: less salt, weight loss, exercise, less alcohol. Drugs when readings stay high or risk is raised: ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium-channel blockers, thiazide-like diuretics, added stepwise; most people need two or more.
hypertension.prevention: A diet rich in fruit, vegetables and low in salt, regular activity, healthy weight, moderate alcohol and no smoking.
hypertension.seekCare: A reading of 180/120 or higher with headache, chest pain, breathlessness, vision change, confusion, weakness or difficulty speaking needs emergency care: call 999 or go to A&E. A reading this high without symptoms needs urgent medical advice from a GP or NHS 111.

deep-vein-thrombosis.name: Deep vein thrombosis
deep-vein-thrombosis.definition: A blood clot in a deep vein, most often of the calf or thigh.
deep-vein-thrombosis.overview: Clots form when blood flow slows, the vein wall is injured or the blood clots too easily (Virchow's triad). A leg DVT causes pain and swelling; its danger is that a fragment can break off and lodge in the lungs as a pulmonary embolism. Most clots start in the deep veins of the calf, where flow is slow; damage to the vein from surgery or injury, and conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes, add to the risk, and pregnancy, ageing and prolonged immobility after an operation or on a long flight are among the commonest triggers. NHS guidance describes the typical leg: swelling, usually at the back of the leg, a throbbing pain or heavy ache in the calf or thigh, skin that is warm or red, and tender, swollen surface veins. Many DVTs cause no symptoms at all, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism are together called venous thromboembolism (VTE), a serious but largely preventable condition.
causes: Immobility: surgery, long flights, bed rest, plaster casts
Cancer and chemotherapy
Pregnancy, the combined pill and hormone replacement
Inherited clotting tendencies (factor V Leiden and others)
Injury to the vein
Damage to the vein wall from surgery or injury
Conditions such as high blood pressure and diabetes
signs: One calf swollen more than 3 cm larger than the other, warm, tender, with dilated surface veins
Warm, red or discoloured skin over the clot
Visibly enlarged surface veins
No abnormal findings in a proportion of cases
complications: Post-thrombotic syndrome: chronic pain and heaviness, swelling, skin discolouration, new varicose veins and in severe cases leg ulcers
deep-vein-thrombosis.diagnosis: The clinician assesses the probability from the history, risk factors and examination, rules out other causes of a swollen leg such as cellulitis, a Baker's cyst, a muscle or joint injury or lymphoedema, and then tests. A D-dimer blood test is used to rule DVT out in low-probability cases; compression ultrasound of the leg veins confirms it. If a pulmonary embolism is suspected, CT angiography images the lung arteries. Because VTE can occur without obvious signs, a low threshold for testing is kept in people with risk factors.
deep-vein-thrombosis.treatment: Anticoagulation for at least three months, usually with a direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, rivaroxaban) or warfarin; compression stockings for symptoms; early mobilisation. Large clots occasionally need catheter-directed clot removal. Anticoagulants do not literally thin the blood; they alter clotting proteins so that new clots form less easily and the existing clot stops extending while the body breaks it down. Compression socks can ease pain and swelling. Clot-dissolving drugs (thrombolysis), mechanical clot removal (thrombectomy) and inferior vena cava filters are less common options used alongside anticoagulation in selected cases. Current guidance does not recommend routine compression stockings to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome, though a trial is reasonable when leg swelling is troublesome.
deep-vein-thrombosis.prevention: Move early after surgery, use prescribed stockings and injections in hospital, walk and hydrate on long journeys, stop smoking. In hospital, people judged to be at higher risk are given preventive anticoagulant medicine or compression stockings.
deep-vein-thrombosis.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a swollen painful calf; emergency care if breathlessness or chest pain develops. NHS guidance is to call 999 or go to A&E if leg symptoms are accompanied by breathlessness or chest pain, since this can mean the clot has travelled to the lungs.

references.title: NHLBI: Venous Thromboembolism - Causes and Risk Factors
NCBI PMC: Guidance for the prevention and treatment of the post-thrombotic syndrome

pulmonary-embolism.name: Pulmonary embolism
pulmonary-embolism.definition: Blockage of a pulmonary artery by a clot that has travelled from a vein, usually in the leg or pelvis.
pulmonary-embolism.overview: A pulmonary embolism cuts off blood flow to part of the lung: the affected segment is ventilated but not perfused, oxygen levels fall and the right ventricle strains against the obstruction. Small emboli cause pleuritic pain and breathlessness; a large one can cause collapse and death within minutes. Symptoms are not specific. Chest pain and breathlessness are the commonest, with dizziness or light-headedness, a fast heartbeat, coughing up blood or collapse also possible, so PE can neither be confirmed nor excluded from symptoms alone, and some emboli cause no symptoms and are found incidentally on a scan. Nearly all cases arise from a deep vein thrombosis in the legs or pelvis. A substantial proportion of cases are 'unprovoked', with no identifiable cause; the rest are 'provoked' by a clear trigger such as surgery, immobility or serious illness, and this distinction shapes how long treatment continues.
causes: Deep vein thrombosis of the leg or pelvis
Rarely fat, air or amniotic fluid emboli
riskFactors: Major surgery, especially gynaecological operations and surgery on the pelvis and legs
signs: Fast breathing and pulse
Low oxygen saturation
Signs of DVT in a leg
Low blood pressure in massive PE
A normal examination does not exclude PE; some emboli are found incidentally on imaging
complications: Significant bleeding in a small proportion of people on anticoagulant treatment
Recurrent clots, more likely when the first was unprovoked or the risk persists
pulmonary-embolism.diagnosis: Probability scoring and D-dimer, then CT pulmonary angiography to show the clot; ventilation-perfusion scanning in pregnancy or kidney disease. ECG and echocardiography assess strain on the right heart. In someone judged at low clinical probability, a negative D-dimer makes PE very unlikely. A positive result is not conclusive, because D-dimer also rises with inflammation and infection, so people at higher risk or with a positive test proceed to lung imaging for a definitive answer.
pulmonary-embolism.treatment: Immediate anticoagulation (low-molecular-weight heparin, then a direct oral anticoagulant or warfarin for three to six months or longer); clot-dissolving drugs or catheter removal for massive PE with shock; oxygen and support. Anticoagulants do not thin the blood or dissolve the clot; they alter clotting so that the clot cannot grow and new clots do not form while the body clears it. The choice of drug depends on kidney function, body weight and other medicines being taken, and significant bleeding occurs in a small proportion of people treated. Clots provoked by a transient risk factor are treated for a limited period, whereas unprovoked clots or persisting risks such as cancer, chronic immobility or a strong clotting disorder may need long-term treatment to prevent recurrence. Oxygen helps breathlessness and low oxygen levels early on. Untreated PE carries a high death rate; with treatment the outlook is much better.
pulmonary-embolism.prevention: DVT prevention: early mobilisation, prophylactic injections in hospital, compression stockings, keeping moving on long journeys.
pulmonary-embolism.seekCare: Emergency services for sudden breathlessness, chest pain on breathing, coughing blood or collapse, especially with a swollen leg or recent surgery.

references.title: NHS Worcestershire Acute Hospitals: Pulmonary embolus diagnosed

stroke.name: Stroke
stroke.definition: Sudden loss of brain function because blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted, by a blocked artery (ischaemic, 85%) or a bleed (haemorrhagic).
stroke.overview: Brain tissue dies within minutes of losing its blood supply, and the lost functions map the artery: weakness and numbness of the opposite side, loss of speech, loss of half the visual field, or unsteadiness and double vision from the brainstem. Treatment to reopen the artery works only in the first hours, so stroke is a medical emergency recognised by the FAST test.
causes: Atherosclerosis of the carotid and cerebral arteries
Emboli from the heart in atrial fibrillation
Small vessel disease from high blood pressure and diabetes
Bleeding from high blood pressure, aneurysms or vascular malformations
Arterial dissection in younger people
signs: Facial droop
Arm drift
Slurred or absent speech
Loss of a visual field
Unsteady gait
stroke.diagnosis: Immediate CT to distinguish a bleed from a blockage, then CT or MR angiography to find the blocked vessel. Blood glucose is checked at once to exclude hypoglycaemia. ECG, echocardiography and carotid ultrasound search for the source.
stroke.treatment: For ischaemic stroke, clot-dissolving thrombolysis within 4.5 hours and mechanical thrombectomy for a large-vessel blockage, as soon as possible (usually within 6 hours of onset, and up to 24 hours in selected people whose scans show brain tissue that can still be saved), then antiplatelet drugs, statins, blood pressure control and anticoagulation if AF is found. Bleeds need blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulants and sometimes surgery. Rehabilitation by a stroke team drives recovery.
stroke.prevention: Treat blood pressure and atrial fibrillation, stop smoking, control diabetes and cholesterol, exercise, and manage weight and alcohol.
stroke.seekCare: Call emergency services immediately at any sign of Face drooping, Arm weakness or Speech difficulty: Time matters. Call 999 even if the symptoms go away: a TIA is a warning that a stroke may follow and needs urgent specialist assessment.

migraine.name: Migraine
migraine.definition: A recurrent headache disorder with attacks of moderate to severe throbbing pain, typically one-sided, lasting 4 to 72 hours, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound.
migraine.overview: Migraine is a disorder of brain excitability rather than of blood vessels alone. A wave of altered activity spreading across the cortex explains the aura that a third of sufferers experience, and activation of the trigeminal pain pathway explains the headache. It affects about one person in seven and is the leading cause of disability in young women. Attacks pass through phases: a prodrome, hours to days beforehand, with food cravings, mood changes or yawning; an aura in some people; the headache itself; and a postdrome. Not every phase occurs in every attack. Aura typically begins within the hour before the headache and usually lasts less than an hour, with visual change, difficulty speaking, tingling in the hands or face or confusion. It is thought to arise from cortical spreading depression, and researchers still debate whether that same process causes the headache. Triggers such as stress or sensory overload usually precede an attack by less than two days, and a headache diary is the practical way to identify an individual's triggers.
causes: Inherited susceptibility with triggers: sleep change, missed meals, stress and stress release, hormones, alcohol, certain foods, bright light, weather
signs: Normal examination between and usually during attacks
complications: Chronic migraine (15 or more headache days a month)
Slightly raised stroke risk in migraine with aura, especially with smoking and the combined pill
Coexistence with, or misdiagnosis as, stroke or transient ischaemic attack, depression and anxiety disorders
migraine.diagnosis: Clinical, from the pattern of attacks; a headache diary helps. Scans are needed only for red-flag features such as a change in pattern, abnormal examination or a thunderclap onset. There is no single confirmatory test. The clinician reviews the health history, performs physical and neurological examinations, and asks when headaches start, how long they last, what they feel like, what triggers them and whether nausea or visual change accompany them. Migraine is often confused with, or coexists with, other conditions including ischaemic stroke and transient ischaemic attack, depression, generalised anxiety and panic disorder, which can complicate the diagnosis.
migraine.treatment: Attacks: a triptan taken early, plus an NSAID or paracetamol and an anti-sickness drug; rest in a dark room. Prevention when attacks are frequent: propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan, CGRP antibody injections, and avoiding identified triggers. Gepants are a newer class used alongside triptans for acute attacks, and painkillers work best taken as soon as the headache starts. Preventive medicine has to be taken every day to be effective, and a combination of treatments is sometimes needed before one works. Migraine cannot be cured, but treatment can manage attacks and reduce their number.
migraine.prevention: Regular sleep and meals, hydration, limiting caffeine and alcohol, exercise, stress management, and limiting painkillers to fewer than 10 days a month. NINDS and the NHS emphasise healthier sleep habits (enough sleep and a consistent bedtime), not skipping meals, avoiding identified food triggers, managing stress and losing weight if overweight.
migraine.seekCare: Emergency care for a headache that is the worst ever or peaks within a minute, or comes with fever, stiff neck, weakness, confusion or a first-ever aura after 50.

epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
epilepsy.definition: A tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures: bursts of abnormal synchronised electrical activity in the brain.
epilepsy.overview: Seizures take many forms depending on where they start: a focal seizure may cause twitching of one hand, an odd smell or a period of unresponsive staring; a generalised tonic-clonic seizure involves loss of consciousness, stiffening and jerking of the whole body. Most people with epilepsy become seizure-free on medication.
causes: Often unknown or genetic
Scarring from stroke, head injury, infection or birth injury
Brain tumours and malformations
Hippocampal sclerosis
Dementia in older people
signs: Usually normal between seizures
Post-seizure confusion, bitten tongue, incontinence
complications: Status epilepticus (a seizure over five minutes: an emergency)
epilepsy.diagnosis: A witness account or video is the most useful evidence. An EEG may show epileptic discharges; MRI looks for a structural cause; blood tests exclude metabolic causes and an ECG excludes a cardiac cause of collapse.
epilepsy.treatment: Anti-seizure medication chosen by seizure type (for example levetiracetam and lamotrigine; valproate is avoided in girls and women who could become pregnant because of the risk to an unborn baby), taken consistently. Surgery, laser ablation or nerve stimulation for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Seizure first aid education for family.
epilepsy.prevention: Take medication regularly, sleep well, limit alcohol, avoid known triggers; helmets and safe driving reduce head injuries that cause acquired epilepsy.
epilepsy.seekCare: Call emergency services for a seizure lasting more than five minutes, repeated seizures without recovery, a first seizure, injury, or difficulty breathing afterwards.

parkinsons-disease.name: Parkinson's disease
parkinsons-disease.definition: A progressive disorder in which dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra of the midbrain are lost, causing slowness, stiffness and tremor.
parkinsons-disease.overview: The basal ganglia need dopamine to release intended movements smoothly. As nigral neurons die, movements become slow and small, muscles stiff, and a resting tremor appears, typically starting on one side. Non-motor features such as loss of smell, constipation, sleep disturbance and later cognitive change are part of the disease. NINDS describes Parkinson's as a chronic, progressive neurological disorder characterised by resting tremor, muscle rigidity, slowness of movement, impaired balance and a shuffling gait. The root causes remain unknown; age, genetics and exposure to environmental hazards are the recognised risk factors. Under the microscope, unusual protein clumps called Lewy bodies form in brain cells. Sleep disorders, constipation and a reduced sense of smell can develop years or even decades before movement problems, and the classical motor features appear only once most of the dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra have already been lost, which is why the diagnosis is often made late.
causes: Accumulation of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein in neurons; the trigger is unknown in most cases
Genetic forms in a minority
Rare toxin exposure
Known genetic variants are rare and each carries only a small risk
riskFactors: Constipation and a history of anxiety or depression as prodromal features
Rural living, farming and well-water drinking
signs: Resting tremor (pill-rolling)
Bradykinesia: slow, small movements
Rigidity (cogwheeling)
Stooped posture, shuffling gait, reduced arm swing
Reduced facial expression, soft voice, small handwriting
complications: Psychosis as a side effect of levodopa in some patients
parkinsons-disease.diagnosis: Clinical, by a neurologist, on the combination of bradykinesia with tremor or rigidity and a response to levodopa. MRI excludes other causes; a DaT scan can confirm dopamine loss when uncertain. Early diagnosis is difficult because early symptoms are often misread as the effects of normal ageing. A large and sustained response to levodopa strongly supports Parkinson's disease over secondary or atypical parkinsonism.
parkinsons-disease.treatment: Levodopa remains the most effective drug; dopamine agonists, MAO-B and COMT inhibitors extend its effect. Physiotherapy, exercise, speech and occupational therapy maintain function. Deep brain stimulation helps selected patients with fluctuations. Levodopa, taken as a tablet or liquid, is combined with benserazide or carbidopa so that it is not broken down in the bloodstream before it reaches the brain. Long-term use is linked to involuntary jerky movements (dyskinesias), 'on-off' effects and wearing-off before the next dose is due, and in some people to psychiatric effects including psychosis. In milder disease clinicians may start with dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors or amantadine to delay levodopa; COMT inhibitors extend its effect. Deep brain stimulation is introduced when medication no longer controls symptoms.
parkinsons-disease.prevention: No proven prevention; regular exercise and coffee are linked to lower risk and exercise slows decline. Caffeine and physical activity appear protective in observational studies, although reverse causation is possible because early disease itself reduces how much people exercise. Smoking is not recommended: the lower rate seen in smokers in these studies does not mean that smoking prevents Parkinson's disease.
parkinsons-disease.seekCare: See a doctor for a new tremor at rest, slowing of movement or a change in gait; urgent help for falls with injury, inability to swallow, or sudden confusion.

references.title: NINDS: AMP Parkinson's Disease and Related Disorders
NCBI PMC: Parkinson's disease updates: pathophysiology, risk factors, genetics, diagnosis, and medical and surgical treatment
NCBI PMC: Meta-Analysis of Early Nonmotor Features and Risk Factors for Parkinson Disease

alzheimers-disease.name: Alzheimer's disease
alzheimers-disease.definition: The commonest cause of dementia: a progressive loss of memory and thinking ability caused by the build-up of amyloid plaques and tau tangles and the death of neurons, beginning in the hippocampus.
alzheimers-disease.overview: Alzheimer's starts years before symptoms, with abnormal proteins accumulating in the medial temporal lobes. Early disease affects the formation of new memories; over years it spreads to language, spatial skills, judgement and finally basic bodily functions. The risk rises steeply with age.
causes: Accumulation of amyloid-beta and tau proteins with loss of synapses and neurons
Rare inherited forms with early onset
riskFactors: Cardiovascular risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, smoking, obesity
Low education, hearing loss, social isolation, depression, inactivity
signs: Poor recall of recent events with preserved distant memory
Word-finding difficulty
Getting lost in familiar places
Impaired judgement and planning
Later: personality change, incontinence, immobility
complications: Infections, especially pneumonia and urinary infections
alzheimers-disease.diagnosis: History from the person and a relative, cognitive testing, blood tests to exclude thyroid, B12 and other reversible causes, and MRI showing hippocampal shrinkage. Amyloid PET or spinal fluid markers can confirm the diagnosis in specialist settings.
alzheimers-disease.treatment: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) and memantine give modest symptomatic benefit; anti-amyloid antibodies give a modest slowing of decline in a small group of people with early disease and can cause brain swelling or bleeding; whether they are available depends on national guidance. Structured routines, cognitive stimulation, treating hearing loss and depression, carer support and advance care planning matter as much.
alzheimers-disease.prevention: Up to 40% of dementia is attributable to modifiable factors: control blood pressure, stay physically, socially and mentally active, treat hearing loss, do not smoke, limit alcohol.
alzheimers-disease.seekCare: Forgetting recent conversations, repeating questions, getting lost or struggling with familiar tasks over months should prompt a memory assessment; sudden confusion over hours or days is delirium and needs urgent review.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.definition: A chronic inflammatory disease of the airways causing reversible narrowing, with episodes of wheeze, breathlessness, chest tightness and cough.
asthma.overview: In asthma the bronchial lining is chronically inflamed and over-reactive. Triggers such as allergens, viruses, exercise or cold air make the smooth muscle constrict and the lining swell and pour out mucus. Between attacks breathing may be normal. It affects about one child in ten and one adult in twelve.
causes: Genetic susceptibility plus environmental exposure: allergens (dust mite, pollen, pets), early viral infections, tobacco smoke, air pollution, occupational chemicals
riskFactors: Family history of asthma or allergy
signs: Widespread wheeze on breathing out
Fast breathing, use of accessory muscles in an attack
A silent chest and exhaustion in a life-threatening attack
complications: Side effects of repeated steroid courses
asthma.diagnosis: Variable symptoms plus evidence of variable airflow obstruction: spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility, peak-flow variability, or raised exhaled nitric oxide and blood eosinophils.
asthma.treatment: Inhaled corticosteroids are the foundation, combined with a long-acting bronchodilator as needed; a reliever inhaler for symptoms; a written action plan; trigger avoidance; biologic injections for severe allergic or eosinophilic asthma. Attacks are treated with high-dose reliever, oral steroids and oxygen.
asthma.prevention: Avoid smoking and smoke exposure, control allergens, have flu vaccination, use the preventer inhaler daily and check inhaler technique.
asthma.seekCare: Emergency care if the reliever is not helping, the person cannot speak in sentences, lips are blue, or peak flow is below a third of best.

copd.name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
copd.definition: Progressive, largely irreversible airflow obstruction caused by damage to the airways (chronic bronchitis) and destruction of alveoli (emphysema), almost always from smoking.
copd.overview: Years of inhaled smoke inflame the small airways and dissolve the alveolar walls, so air is trapped and the surface for gas exchange shrinks. Breathlessness on exertion creeps up over decades and is often blamed on age; flare-ups triggered by infections drive hospital admissions. COPD is the third leading cause of death worldwide.
causes: Tobacco smoking (85 to 90% of cases)
Biomass and cooking-fire smoke
Occupational dust and fumes
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (inherited)
riskFactors: Childhood respiratory infections and poor lung growth
signs: Barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing
Wheeze and reduced breath sounds
Cyanosis and ankle oedema in advanced disease
complications: Pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale)
copd.diagnosis: Spirometry showing an FEV1/FVC ratio below 0.7 that does not fully reverse with a bronchodilator, in someone with symptoms and a smoking or exposure history. Chest X-ray and CT exclude other causes and grade emphysema.
copd.treatment: Stopping smoking is the only measure that slows decline. Long-acting bronchodilator inhalers (with inhaled steroids for frequent exacerbators), pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, and oxygen at home for low oxygen levels. Exacerbations are treated with steroids and often antibiotics.
copd.prevention: Never smoking, or stopping at any stage; clean cooking fuels; workplace dust control; vaccination against flu, pneumococcus and COVID-19.
copd.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for severe breathlessness, blue lips, chest pain, or new confusion or drowsiness (a sign of carbon dioxide retention). Get same-day advice from a GP or NHS 111 for worsening breathlessness with more or discoloured sputum, or fever.

pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
pneumonia.definition: Infection of the alveoli, which fill with fluid and inflammatory cells so that part of the lung cannot exchange gas.
pneumonia.overview: Bacteria (most often Streptococcus pneumoniae), viruses (influenza, COVID-19, RSV) and occasionally fungi cause pneumonia. It ranges from a mild illness treated at home to a life-threatening one in the elderly, the very young and those with chronic disease, and it remains the leading infectious cause of death in children worldwide.
causes: Bacteria: pneumococcus, Haemophilus, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Staphylococcus
Viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, RSV
Aspiration of stomach contents
Hospital-acquired organisms in ventilated or frail patients
riskFactors: Weak immune system, diabetes, heart, kidney or liver disease
signs: Fast breathing, fever, crackles and dull percussion over the affected lobe
Low oxygen saturation
Confusion in the elderly
pneumonia.diagnosis: Clinical findings plus a chest X-ray showing consolidation. Blood tests (white cells, CRP, kidney function), oxygen saturation, sputum and blood cultures, and a severity score (CURB-65) guide where and how to treat.
pneumonia.treatment: Antibiotics chosen by likely organism and severity (amoxicillin for mild community-acquired pneumonia; combinations in hospital), antivirals for influenza, oxygen, fluids, and support of breathing in severe cases. Rest and hydration at home for mild cases.
pneumonia.prevention: Pneumococcal, influenza and COVID-19 vaccination, stopping smoking, good hand hygiene, and managing chronic diseases.
pneumonia.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness at rest, confusion, blue lips, chest pain, coughing blood, or fever with fast breathing in a child or older adult.

lung-cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour arising from the lining of the airways or alveoli, divided into non-small-cell (about 85%) and small-cell types.
lung-cancer.overview: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death because it is usually found late: symptoms appear only when a tumour blocks an airway, invades the chest wall or spreads. Smoking causes about eight in ten cases. Low-dose CT screening of eligible heavy smokers can find lung cancer at an earlier stage, when treatment is more likely to be curative. Early lung cancer often causes no symptoms at all. The NHS lists a persistent cough, breathlessness, coughing up blood and chest or shoulder pain as the main features; less common ones are swelling of the face or neck, difficulty swallowing from pressure on the oesophagus, a hoarse voice that does not go away from pressure on the laryngeal nerves, and clubbing of the fingers. Bone pain and facial or eyelid changes tend to appear late. The cause is not always known: lifestyle, genetic changes and environmental factors all contribute, with smoking the largest single risk. A targeted screening programme using low-dose CT is being rolled out in England for eligible older adults, aimed at finding cancer before symptoms appear.
causes: Tobacco smoke
Radon gas
Asbestos, diesel exhaust and other occupational carcinogens
Air pollution
Family history
Arsenic and other industrial chemicals
signs: Finger clubbing
Hoarse voice
Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck
Signs of a pleural effusion or collapsed lobe
Weight loss
Swelling of the face or neck
Wheeze, or difficulty swallowing from a tumour pressing on the oesophagus
Bone pain and facial or eyelid changes in late disease
complications: Spread to lymph nodes, liver, bones, brain and adrenals
Compression of the oesophagus (swallowing difficulty) and of the laryngeal nerves (hoarseness)
lung-cancer.diagnosis: Chest X-ray then CT of the chest and abdomen; tissue by bronchoscopy or CT-guided biopsy; PET-CT for staging; molecular tests on the tumour to guide targeted therapy. A GP asks about symptoms and general health and may check lung function with a spirometer. A chest X-ray is usually the first test but cannot give a definitive answer on its own, so a specialist arranges a CT scan and a bronchoscopy, in which a thin tube with a camera is passed through the mouth or nose into the airways to take a biopsy that shows the cancer type; a PET-CT scan shows where active cancer cells are. Pathology is reviewed by a specialist lung cancer pathologist before treatment because small-cell cancer can be mistaken for other types. Staging uses the TNM system (tumour size, lymph node spread, distant metastasis) and tells the team whether a complete cure is possible; small-cell cancer is described as limited stage when confined to one half of the chest within a single radiotherapy field, otherwise extensive stage.
lung-cancer.treatment: Depends on type and stage: surgery or radical radiotherapy for early non-small-cell cancer; chemotherapy, immunotherapy and targeted drugs (for EGFR, ALK and other mutations) for advanced disease; chemotherapy and radiotherapy for small-cell cancer; palliative care for symptoms throughout. The choice depends on the type, size and position of the cancer, whether it has spread, specific genetic changes and the person's general health. Surgery is the main curative treatment for non-small-cell cancer and may be combined with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy. Small-cell cancer responds well to chemotherapy and is generally not treated surgically. Radiotherapy can cause breathlessness and a hoarse cough during treatment, which usually ease in the weeks afterwards.
lung-cancer.prevention: Not smoking is the single most effective measure; radon testing of homes; workplace protection; CT screening for eligible heavy smokers.
lung-cancer.seekCare: NHS advice is to see a GP for a cough lasting longer than three weeks, unexplained breathlessness, weight loss or a new hoarse voice, especially with a history of smoking; coughing up blood warrants an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111; and struggling to breathe or pain in the chest or upper back warrants 999 or A&E. Anyone with symptoms is advised not to wait for a screening appointment.

references.title: NHS: Lung cancer - Tests and next steps
National Cancer Institute: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Treatment (PDQ) - Patient Version

appendicitis.name: Appendicitis
appendicitis.definition: Acute inflammation of the appendix, usually because its opening into the caecum is blocked.
appendicitis.overview: The appendix is a blind pouch hanging off the caecum in the lower right abdomen. When its lumen is obstructed, by a hard pellet of stool, swollen lymphoid tissue or rarely a tumour, bacteria multiply, pressure rises, the wall becomes inflamed and, within a day or two, can perforate. It is the commonest cause of emergency abdominal surgery. The classic story is pain that begins around the navel and, over hours, shifts to the lower right abdomen, becoming sharper and worse with movement, coughing or sneezing; loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, a low fever and abdominal swelling commonly follow. The picture is less typical in young children, older adults and pregnant women, in whom the diagnosis is often delayed. NIDDK notes that the cause is usually thought to be multifactorial and that in many cases no specific obstruction is identified.
causes: Obstruction of the appendix lumen by a faecolith or enlarged lymphoid tissue
Rarely a tumour or parasite
Multifactorial in many cases; often no specific cause is found
signs: Tenderness and guarding at McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant
Rebound tenderness
Pain on the right when the left side is pressed (Rovsing's sign)
Mild fever and fast pulse
Abdominal swelling and reluctance to move
complications: Delayed diagnosis in children, older adults and pregnancy, raising the chance of rupture
appendicitis.diagnosis: Largely clinical: the migrating pain, right lower quadrant tenderness and raised white cells and CRP. Clinicians take a history and examine the abdomen, then use urine tests to exclude a urinary infection or kidney stone, blood tests for inflammation, and a pregnancy test in women to exclude an ectopic pregnancy. Imaging confirms the diagnosis or finds another cause of the pain: ultrasound first in children and in pregnancy, CT in adults when the picture is unclear, and MRI where radiation is to be avoided.
appendicitis.treatment: Prompt removal of the appendix (appendectomy), now usually laparoscopic, with antibiotics before and, if perforated, after surgery. Selected uncomplicated cases can be treated with antibiotics alone, with a risk of recurrence. An abscess may be drained first and the appendix removed later. Prompt surgery lowers the risk of rupture. Appendicectomy is performed laparoscopically through small incisions or, when needed, through an open incision (laparotomy), with antibiotics given before surgery and continued afterwards if the appendix has perforated. A ruptured appendix, an abscess or peritonitis needs specialised care: an abscess may be drained under imaging guidance and the appendix removed at a later date.
appendicitis.prevention: None proven. Because appendicitis cannot be prevented, outcomes depend on early recognition and prompt surgery before the appendix ruptures.
appendicitis.seekCare: Same-day emergency assessment for pain that moves to the lower right abdomen, worsens over hours, and comes with nausea, loss of appetite or fever. Severe pain with a high fever may mean the appendix has ruptured and needs immediate hospital care; untreated appendicitis can progress to peritonitis or an abscess, so people are advised not to wait to see whether the pain passes.

gerd.name: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
gerd.definition: Reflux of stomach acid into the oesophagus often enough to cause symptoms or damage the lining.
gerd.overview: The lower oesophageal sphincter normally keeps acid in the stomach. When it relaxes too often or is weakened, especially with a hiatus hernia or obesity, acid burns the unprotected oesophagus. Heartburn after meals and lying down is the classic symptom; chronic reflux can scar the oesophagus or change its lining (Barrett's oesophagus), a precursor of cancer. The anti-reflux barrier is made up of the lower oesophageal sphincter and the crura of the diaphragm that wrap around it; transient relaxations of the sphincter are the commonest mechanism of reflux, with a hiatus hernia, raised abdominal pressure and poor clearance of refluxed acid from the oesophagus adding to it. Heartburn and regurgitation are the typical symptoms, but reflux can also present with chronic cough, asthma, laryngitis or dental erosion in the absence of heartburn, which makes it harder to recognise. Large or late meals, irregular meal timing, smoking, obesity and some medicines all contribute; the evidence linking specific foods is limited and varies between individuals.
causes: Weak or over-relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter
Hiatus hernia
Raised abdominal pressure: obesity, pregnancy
Delayed stomach emptying
Transient relaxations of the lower oesophageal sphincter
Poor clearance of refluxed acid from the oesophagus
riskFactors: Alcohol, coffee, fatty and spicy food, large late meals
Some drugs: NSAIDs, calcium-channel blockers, nitrates
signs: Usually none
Dental erosion, hoarseness
gerd.diagnosis: Typical symptoms responding to acid suppression are usually enough. Endoscopy is done for alarm features (difficulty swallowing, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, onset over 55) or persistent symptoms; pH monitoring quantifies reflux when the diagnosis is unclear. Other causes of similar symptoms, such as eosinophilic oesophagitis, are considered. Upper endoscopy is recommended when alarm features are present or when symptoms do not respond to a proton pump inhibitor; it shows oesophagitis, strictures and Barrett's change and allows biopsy. Oesophageal pH monitoring confirms abnormal acid exposure when the diagnosis remains unclear.
gerd.treatment: Weight loss, smaller earlier meals, raising the bed head, avoiding triggers, stopping smoking. Antacids and alginates for occasional symptoms; proton pump inhibitors for regular symptoms and healing. Anti-reflux surgery (fundoplication) for severe cases. Lifestyle changes are a core part of management and can sometimes control symptoms on their own: dietary adjustments, raising the head of the bed, not lying down soon after eating and stopping smoking. Proton pump inhibitors are the standard first-line medicine; concerns about long-term side effects and about symptoms returning when they are stopped have driven research into newer drugs. Symptoms that persist despite a proton pump inhibitor (refractory reflux) prompt further evaluation to exclude other causes before escalating; endoscopic therapies and anti-reflux surgery such as fundoplication help people whose symptoms are clearly reflux-triggered.
gerd.prevention: Healthy weight, not smoking, moderate alcohol and coffee, no large meals within three hours of bed.
gerd.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for vomiting blood, black or tarry stools, collapse, or chest pain that could be cardiac. See a GP promptly for difficulty or pain swallowing, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting, or heartburn that persists despite treatment.

references.title: NCBI PMC: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD): Highlighting Diagnosis, Treatment, and Lifestyle Changes
NCBI PMC: Current Advances in Diagnosis, Therapeutics, and Surgical Interventions for the Management of Refractory GERD

peptic-ulcer.name: Peptic ulcer
peptic-ulcer.definition: A break in the lining of the stomach or duodenum that extends through the mucosa, caused by acid acting on a weakened defence.
peptic-ulcer.overview: Most peptic ulcers are caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori or by NSAID painkillers, both of which strip the mucus barrier that protects the lining from acid. Duodenal ulcers are commoner and classically hurt when hungry; gastric ulcers hurt after eating. Ulcers can bleed or perforate. Only a minority of people infected with H. pylori go on to develop ulcer disease. Symptoms include pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen, feeling full too soon during or too full after a meal, nausea, bloating and belching, though some people have no pain and small ulcers may cause no symptoms at all. Bleeding can be slow and subtle, so the only clue may be tiredness and weakness from anaemia rather than visible blood. As awareness and treatment of H. pylori have grown, bleeding ulcers are increasingly linked to NSAID use, older age and other illnesses.
causes: Helicobacter pylori infection
NSAIDs and aspirin
Rarely: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, severe physiological stress, Crohn's disease
riskFactors: Steroids and anticoagulants taken with NSAIDs
Other illnesses (comorbidity) in older people, now a leading context for bleeding ulcers
signs: Epigastric tenderness
Signs of anaemia if bleeding chronically
Rigid abdomen if perforated
Pallor and tiredness from slow blood loss
Early fullness, bloating and belching reported in the history
complications: Bleeding: vomiting blood or passing black stools
peptic-ulcer.diagnosis: Testing for H. pylori (breath, stool or blood test); endoscopy to see the ulcer, take biopsies and treat bleeding, especially in those over 55 or with alarm features. Testing for H. pylori is advised for anyone with a current or past ulcer, or with stomach discomfort lasting more than a month. At endoscopy a rapid urease test on a biopsy, with or without histology, is usually the first test; if it is negative, a urea breath test or serology follows. An upper GI contrast series is an alternative where endoscopy is not performed.
peptic-ulcer.treatment: Eradicate H. pylori with a proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics for one to two weeks; stop NSAIDs; proton pump inhibitor for four to eight weeks to heal. Bleeding ulcers are treated endoscopically; perforation needs surgery. Eradicating H. pylori heals the ulcer and reduces the chance of rebleeding. For NSAID-related ulcers the NSAID is stopped and acid suppression given; if the NSAID cannot be stopped, a proton pump inhibitor is continued alongside it, and misoprostol or a lining-protecting medicine such as sucralfate may be added. Prescribed aspirin or NSAIDs are not stopped without medical advice, since they may need adjusting rather than withdrawal.
peptic-ulcer.prevention: Avoid NSAIDs when possible or take a protective proton pump inhibitor with them, stop smoking, limit alcohol.
peptic-ulcer.seekCare: Emergency care for vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stools, sudden severe abdominal pain, or collapse. MedlinePlus lists sudden sharp abdominal pain, a hard, rigid, tender abdomen, fainting, heavy sweating or confusion, vomiting blood, and maroon or black tarry stools as reasons for urgent care.

references.title: NIDDK: Peptic Ulcers (Stomach or Duodenal Ulcers)

gallstones.name: Gallstones
gallstones.definition: Hard deposits, usually of cholesterol, that form in the gallbladder when bile becomes supersaturated.
gallstones.overview: Gallstones are present in about one adult in ten and most cause no trouble. Symptoms begin when a stone blocks the gallbladder outlet (biliary colic), inflames the gallbladder (cholecystitis), or escapes into the bile duct where it causes jaundice, infection of the bile (cholangitis) or pancreatitis. Bile is a mixture of cholesterol, bile pigment (bilirubin) and bile salts; stones form when it holds too much cholesterol or bilirubin, or too few bile salts to keep them dissolved. Only a minority of people with silent stones ever develop symptoms. When a stone lodges in the gallbladder outlet or a bile duct the result is biliary colic: a sudden, severe pain in the upper abdomen that lasts for hours and then eases. Nausea, indigestion and bloating on their own are not specific to gallstones. Persistent pain with fever or jaundice means the gallbladder has become inflamed or a stone has moved into the bile duct.
causes: Cholesterol supersaturation of bile with sluggish gallbladder emptying
Pigment stones from red cell breakdown (haemolysis) or infection
Too little bile salt or excess bilirubin in bile
signs: Right upper quadrant tenderness worse on breathing in (Murphy's sign)
Fever in cholecystitis
Jaundice with a duct stone
gallstones.diagnosis: Ultrasound shows stones and a thickened gallbladder wall; liver function tests and lipase detect duct obstruction and pancreatitis; MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound finds duct stones. Clinicians combine the history, examination and tests: blood tests show inflammation or infection and whether the bile ducts, gallbladder, pancreas or liver are affected, and ultrasound is the first imaging investigation because it shows stones, gallbladder wall thickening and duct dilatation without radiation.
gallstones.treatment: Silent stones need no treatment. Symptomatic stones: laparoscopic removal of the gallbladder (cholecystectomy), ideally within days of a cholecystitis attack; duct stones are removed endoscopically (ERCP). Pain relief, fluids and antibiotics for infection. NIDDK describes removal of the gallbladder as the usual treatment for symptomatic stones, and almost all are now done laparoscopically. Non-surgical treatment with medicines to dissolve cholesterol stones is sometimes used when surgery is not possible, but pigment stones do not dissolve and need surgery.
gallstones.prevention: Healthy weight lost gradually, regular meals, a diet high in fibre and low in refined carbohydrate.
gallstones.seekCare: Urgent assessment for abdominal pain lasting more than a few hours, pain with fever or shivering, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. A stone blocking the bile duct causes sudden pain that needs medical attention right away.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.definition: Chronic inflammation of the gut driven by an abnormal immune response: ulcerative colitis affects the colon's lining continuously from the rectum; Crohn's disease can affect any part of the tract, in patches and through the full wall thickness.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.overview: IBD typically begins in the teens and twenties and follows a relapsing course. Ulcerative colitis brings bloody diarrhoea and urgency; Crohn's brings pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, mouth ulcers and complications such as strictures and fistulas. Modern immune-modulating drugs control most cases, but surgery is still needed by many.
causes: Interaction of genes, the gut microbiome and an over-active mucosal immune response
Over 200 susceptibility genes identified
riskFactors: Smoking (for Crohn's; it is protective in ulcerative colitis)
NSAIDs and antibiotics may trigger flares
signs: Weight loss, anaemia
Abdominal tenderness or a mass
Perianal fistulas and skin tags in Crohn's
Mouth ulcers, eye inflammation, joint swelling
inflammatory-bowel-disease.diagnosis: Blood tests (anaemia, CRP), faecal calprotectin to distinguish from irritable bowel, stool cultures to exclude infection, colonoscopy with biopsies, and MRI of the small bowel for Crohn's.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.treatment: Aminosalicylates for mild ulcerative colitis; steroids to settle flares; thiopurines, methotrexate and biologic antibodies (anti-TNF, anti-integrin, anti-IL-23) or JAK inhibitors to maintain remission; nutritional therapy in Crohn's; surgery for complications or refractory colitis.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.prevention: No known prevention; not smoking reduces Crohn's flares and complications.
inflammatory-bowel-disease.seekCare: Urgent care for more than six bloody stools a day with fever or a fast pulse, severe abdominal pain and distension, or inability to keep fluids down.

colorectal-cancer.name: Colorectal (bowel) cancer
colorectal-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour of the colon or rectum, almost always arising from a benign polyp (adenoma) over years.
colorectal-cancer.overview: Bowel cancer is the third commonest cancer worldwide. Because it grows slowly from polyps, screening by stool testing and colonoscopy can find and remove growths before they turn malignant. Early cancers are cured by surgery; symptoms usually appear late, so screening participation matters. Early cancers may produce no symptoms, which is why screening is offered to people who feel well: it finds cancers at the stage when treatment is most effective and removes precancerous polyps before they turn malignant. Where symptoms occur they depend on where the tumour sits and whether it has spread, and all of them, including bleeding and a change in bowel habit, also occur in benign conditions, so they are not diagnostic on their own. Treatment is planned by stage, from stage 0 (confined to the lining) to stage IV (spread to distant organs), and the cancer can recur after treatment, so follow-up continues for years.
causes: Accumulated genetic mutations in the lining cells, usually sporadic
Inherited syndromes: Lynch syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis
riskFactors: Processed and red meat, low fibre, obesity, inactivity
A personal history of adenomas (polyps) or a previous bowel cancer
signs: Change in bowel habit lasting weeks
Blood in or on the stool
Iron-deficiency anaemia
A palpable mass
Weight loss
Narrower stools, diarrhoea or constipation persisting for weeks
complications: Spread to liver, lungs and peritoneum
colorectal-cancer.diagnosis: Faecal immunochemical test for screening or triage, then colonoscopy with biopsy; CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging; MRI of the rectum; blood CEA marker. Screening uses a faecal immunochemical test (FIT) that detects hidden blood in the stool; a positive test or new symptoms lead to colonoscopy, which allows the whole colon to be inspected, polyps removed and the tumour biopsied. Once cancer is confirmed, staging determines treatment: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis looks for spread to the liver and lungs, MRI of the pelvis defines how far a rectal cancer has grown through the wall and towards nearby structures, and the blood marker CEA gives a baseline for follow-up.
colorectal-cancer.treatment: Surgery to remove the tumour and lymph nodes is the mainstay; chemotherapy after surgery for higher-risk disease; radiotherapy and chemotherapy before surgery for rectal cancer; chemotherapy, targeted and immune drugs for spread; liver metastases are sometimes resectable. The National Cancer Institute's PDQ summary describes surgery as the most common treatment at every stage. For stage 0 a polypectomy or local excision with clear margins may be enough, with colon resection for larger lesions; for stages I and II the standard operation is wide resection of the affected segment with its lymph nodes and rejoining of the bowel (anastomosis). Chemotherapy after surgery is the established approach for stage III disease and is still under evaluation for stage II. Rectal cancer is often treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy before surgery to shrink the tumour. For stage IV and recurrent disease the options include surgery, systemic chemotherapy, targeted and immune therapies and clinical trials; liver metastases may be treated by resection, chemotherapy before or after surgery, local ablation or chemotherapy delivered into the hepatic artery.
colorectal-cancer.prevention: Take part in screening from the age offered, eat fibre and less processed meat, keep active and a healthy weight, do not smoke, limit alcohol; aspirin lowers risk in Lynch syndrome. Diet, body weight and physical activity have some of the strongest links to risk of any cancer type, so these are the modifiable factors with the most to gain.
colorectal-cancer.seekCare: See a doctor within days for blood in the stool, a change in bowel habit lasting three weeks, unexplained weight loss or anaemia; emergency care for severe pain with vomiting and a swollen abdomen.

references.title: National Cancer Institute: Colon Cancer Treatment (PDQ) - Patient Version
National Cancer Institute: Colon Cancer Treatment (PDQ) - Health Professional Version
NCBI PMC: Colorectal Cancer: Advances in Prevention and Early Detection

cirrhosis.name: Cirrhosis
cirrhosis.definition: Scarring of the liver from long-term damage, in which nodules of regenerating cells are surrounded by fibrous bands that distort blood flow and impair function.
cirrhosis.overview: Years of injury from alcohol, fatty liver disease or viral hepatitis replace liver tissue with scar. The result is failure of the liver's jobs (jaundice, bleeding, confusion) and high pressure in the portal vein (varices, fluid in the abdomen, an enlarged spleen). Stopping or treating the cause can slow or halt further scarring and may allow some recovery, but complications and the risk of liver cancer can persist, so follow-up continues. Cirrhosis is the final stage of chronic liver disease: scar tissue replaces healthy tissue and stops the liver working normally. Early on it often causes nothing noticeable, and it is sometimes found by chance on an abdominal ultrasound or on blood tests taken for another reason. As it progresses people report fatigue, itchy skin, poor appetite, unintended weight loss and swelling of the legs and ankles, then fluid in the abdomen (ascites) and yellowing of the eyes and skin (jaundice). Hepatic encephalopathy, confusion caused by the failing liver no longer clearing toxins, can progress to unconsciousness. Some people have more than one cause at the same time, for example alcohol and fatty liver disease.
causes: Alcohol
Metabolic dysfunction-associated (fatty) liver disease
Hepatitis B and C
Autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis
Haemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Some medicines (drug-induced liver injury)
More than one cause acting together
riskFactors: Unprotected sex or injected drug use (viral hepatitis)
signs: Jaundice, spider naevi, red palms
Enlarged spleen, ascites
Muscle wasting, bruising
Confusion and a flapping tremor (encephalopathy)
Oedema of the legs and ankles
Itching and scratch marks
complications: Malnutrition, weight loss and muscle wasting
cirrhosis.diagnosis: Liver function tests, clotting and platelet count; ultrasound or elastography (FibroScan) measuring stiffness; tests for the cause (hepatitis viruses, iron, autoantibodies); endoscopy for varices; six-monthly ultrasound for cancer surveillance. The diagnosis rests on history, examination and test results together: blood tests show liver damage, reduced synthetic function and infection; imaging shows a nodular liver, an enlarged spleen and ascites; elastography measures stiffness without a needle, so liver biopsy is reserved for cases where the cause or stage remains uncertain.
cirrhosis.treatment: Remove the cause: complete abstinence from alcohol, weight loss, antivirals for hepatitis B and C. Diuretics for ascites, beta blockers or banding for varices, lactulose for encephalopathy, nutrition, vaccination. Liver transplantation for decompensated disease. No treatment reverses established cirrhosis, but treating the disease that caused it may stop it getting worse and prevent liver failure: antiviral medicines for hepatitis B and C, steroid medicines for autoimmune hepatitis, abstinence for alcohol-related disease and weight loss for fatty liver disease. Complications are managed as they arise with medicines for abdominal and leg swelling, for encephalopathy and for dilated oesophageal veins, and with surveillance imaging for liver cancer. Vaccination protects against hepatitis B, one of the leading causes. Liver transplantation is considered for advanced, decompensated disease.
cirrhosis.prevention: Drink within recommended limits or not at all, keep a healthy weight, vaccinate against hepatitis B, never share needles, treat hepatitis C. Hepatitis B vaccination prevents one of the leading causes outright.
cirrhosis.seekCare: Emergency care for vomiting blood, black stools, confusion or drowsiness, a rapidly swelling abdomen with fever, or deepening jaundice. MedlinePlus advises emergency help for sudden abdominal or chest pain in someone with cirrhosis, and prompt contact with a clinician for any new symptom suggesting the disease.

references.title: MedlinePlus: Cirrhosis
references.section: Causes; When to contact a medical professional

pancreatitis.name: Pancreatitis
pancreatitis.definition: Inflammation of the pancreas, acute when its own enzymes are activated inside the gland, chronic when repeated injury leads to scarring and loss of function.
pancreatitis.overview: Gallstones and alcohol cause four in five cases of acute pancreatitis. Activated enzymes digest the gland and surrounding fat, and severe cases trigger a body-wide inflammatory response with organ failure. Most attacks are mild and settle in days; chronic pancreatitis causes lasting pain, malabsorption and diabetes. Acute pancreatitis is short-term and often resolves within days with treatment; chronic pancreatitis worsens over time, causes lasting damage and can follow one or more acute attacks. In an acute attack, upper abdominal pain spreads to the back with nausea and vomiting; fever and a fast pulse are common and, in severe cases, blood pressure falls, dehydration develops and organ failure, internal bleeding or death can follow. Chronic disease presents differently, with nausea, weight loss and oily stools, because digestive enzymes such as trypsin no longer reach the gut in adequate amounts. A gallstone lodging in the common bile duct blocks pancreatic drainage; alcohol is the leading cause of chronic disease.
causes: Gallstones blocking the duct
Alcohol
High triglycerides, high calcium
Some drugs (azathioprine, valproate, thiazides)
After ERCP
Viral infections, trauma, genetic mutations
Cystic fibrosis and other inherited disorders
Autoimmune pancreatitis
Injury or surgery to the pancreas; infections such as mumps; lupus
signs: Severe epigastric tenderness
Fast pulse, low blood pressure in severe disease
Bruising of the flanks or around the navel in haemorrhagic cases
Jaundice with a duct stone
Dehydration
Weight loss and oily stools in chronic disease
complications: Organ failure and death in severe attacks
Diabetes and malabsorption in chronic disease
Pancreatic cancer risk in chronic pancreatitis
pancreatitis.diagnosis: Typical pain with a serum lipase or amylase more than three times normal; ultrasound for gallstones; CT after 48 to 72 hours if severe to assess necrosis; blood tests to score severity. In NHS practice acute pancreatitis is usually diagnosed from blood tests, with a CT scan in some cases, and further tests are then run to identify the underlying cause so it can be treated.
pancreatitis.treatment: Intravenous fluids, pain relief, early feeding when tolerated; ERCP to remove a duct stone with cholangitis; antibiotics and drainage for infected necrosis; cholecystectomy before discharge for gallstone pancreatitis. Chronic disease: stop alcohol and smoking, enzyme supplements, pain management, diabetes care. Treatment in hospital includes fluids and nutrients given through a tube into a vein, painkillers, and antibiotics if an infection develops; most people start to improve within a week. Early feeding is favoured because early enteral nutrition has been shown to improve outcomes. For gallstone pancreatitis the gallbladder is removed during the same admission or soon afterwards to limit the risk of recurrence; alcohol-related disease improves with stopping alcohol and treatment for dependency. Surgery is reserved for complications.
pancreatitis.prevention: Moderate alcohol, treat gallstones once symptomatic, control triglycerides, stop smoking.
pancreatitis.seekCare: Emergency care for severe constant upper abdominal pain radiating to the back with vomiting, especially after alcohol or with known gallstones.

references.title: NHS Guy's and St Thomas': Acute pancreatitis - Overview

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.definition: The commonest joint disease: progressive loss of articular cartilage with changes in the underlying bone, causing pain and stiffness, most often in the knees, hips, hands and spine.
osteoarthritis.overview: Osteoarthritis is not simply wear: it is a failed repair process in which cartilage thins, bone thickens and forms spurs (osteophytes), and the joint lining becomes intermittently inflamed. Pain builds over years, worse with use and at the end of the day. It affects most people over 65 to some degree. Pain and stiffness are the hallmark. Early on, symptoms may appear only after exercise, but over time they can become constant, and they often come and go in episodes related to activity levels and even the weather. Swelling, a reduced range of motion and weakness or wasting of the muscles around the joint also occur. The joints most often affected are those near the ends of the fingers, the base of the thumb, the neck, the lower back, the knees and the hips. The disease is thought to stem from mechanical stress on the joint combined with low-grade inflammation, and the problems usually come on over years.
causes: Mechanical load on a susceptible joint: age, previous injury, malalignment, obesity
Genetic factors, especially in hand OA
Abnormal development or alignment of the joint or limb
riskFactors: Heavy manual work or elite sport
signs: Bony enlargement, crepitus, reduced range of motion
Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes on the fingers
Effusion in a flared knee
Antalgic gait
Weakness or wasting of the muscles around the affected joint
osteoarthritis.diagnosis: Clinical in a person over 45 with activity-related pain and brief morning stiffness. X-rays show joint-space narrowing, sclerosis and osteophytes but correlate poorly with symptoms; blood tests are normal and are used to exclude inflammatory arthritis. Early joint damage does not usually show on X-ray. MRI shows soft-tissue damage and is especially useful when a joint locks or gives way. Blood tests and joint-fluid sampling are used to rule out other causes such as infection or gout rather than to confirm osteoarthritis.
osteoarthritis.treatment: Exercise and strengthening, weight loss, education and pacing are the core treatments. Topical NSAIDs, paracetamol and oral NSAIDs for pain; walking aids and braces; steroid injections for flares. Joint replacement when pain limits life despite these. There is no cure. The NHS describes three main strands: lifestyle measures, medicines to relieve pain, and supportive therapies that make everyday activities easier; surgery is considered only in some cases where other treatments have not helped. Regular exercise that keeps a person active, builds up muscle and strengthens the joints usually improves symptoms. NIAMS advises starting slowly with a plan from a doctor or physiotherapist that combines range-of-motion and stretching work with strengthening using weights or resistance bands, to reduce pain and stiffness and increase flexibility, strength and endurance.
osteoarthritis.prevention: Healthy weight, regular low-impact exercise, strong muscles around the joints, and avoiding joint injury.
osteoarthritis.seekCare: See a doctor for joint pain limiting daily activities; urgent care for a hot, red, swollen joint with fever.

rheumatoid-arthritis.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
rheumatoid-arthritis.definition: A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovial lining of joints, causing symmetrical inflammation that can destroy cartilage and bone.
rheumatoid-arthritis.overview: Rheumatoid arthritis typically starts in the small joints of the hands and feet with prolonged morning stiffness and swelling, and can involve the eyes, lungs, heart and blood vessels. Untreated it deforms and disables; started early, disease-modifying drugs now prevent most damage. Arthritis is the cardinal feature, but extra-articular disease is common: interstitial lung disease is among the most frequent manifestations and is more likely in smokers, in men and in people positive for anti-CCP antibodies and rheumatoid factor. Treatment with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) is recommended early for every patient because it slows joint destruction and prevents deformity, although these medicines carry considerable side effects and cost.

structures: Proximal phalanx of right index finger

causes: Autoimmunity against citrullinated proteins, in genetically susceptible people, often triggered by smoking or infection
riskFactors: Smoking, male sex and antibody positivity raise the risk of lung involvement
signs: Symmetrical swelling of metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints
Morning stiffness over an hour
Rheumatoid nodules
Later: ulnar deviation, swan-neck deformities
complications: Interstitial lung disease, the most common form of lung involvement
Drug toxicity: marrow suppression, infection, liver damage and pneumonitis with methotrexate
rheumatoid-arthritis.diagnosis: Clinical pattern plus rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, raised CRP and ESR, and ultrasound or X-ray showing synovitis and erosions. Early referral to rheumatology within weeks changes outcomes. Lung involvement is diagnosed from clinical and radiological findings, and pulmonary function tests may show a restrictive pattern.
rheumatoid-arthritis.treatment: Methotrexate started early, with short-term steroids to control symptoms; biologic drugs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6, B-cell depletion) or JAK inhibitors if disease stays active; NSAIDs for pain; physiotherapy, occupational therapy and cardiovascular risk management. Methotrexate is the most commonly used DMARD, with leflunomide and hydroxychloroquine as alternatives; it reduces pain and X-ray joint damage, but a substantial minority of patients do not respond well despite optimal dosing. DMARDs fall into three groups: conventional synthetic (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine), targeted synthetic (JAK inhibitors) and biologic (TNF and IL-6 inhibitors). Methotrexate can suppress the bone marrow and cause serious infections, liver damage, mouth and skin problems and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. NSAIDs reduce swelling and pain well but do not prevent joint damage, so they are used for short periods at low doses alongside a DMARD.
rheumatoid-arthritis.prevention: Not smoking and good dental health reduce risk; early treatment prevents damage.
rheumatoid-arthritis.seekCare: See a doctor within weeks for swelling of several joints with morning stiffness; urgent care for a single hot joint with fever or new neck pain with tingling in the arms.
