osteoporosis.name: Osteoporosis
osteoporosis.definition: Loss of bone mass and deterioration of bone architecture that makes bones fragile and prone to fracture after minimal trauma.
osteoporosis.overview: Bone is constantly remodelled; after the peak mass reached around 30, resorption slowly outpaces formation, sharply so in women after the menopause. Osteoporosis is silent until a bone breaks: the wrist, spine or hip. Hip fractures in older adults carry a high risk of death and loss of independence, and are largely preventable. It is the major cause of fractures in postmenopausal women and in older men, and is often called a silent disease: there are no symptoms until a bone breaks, so it is frequently diagnosed only when a fall or sudden impact causes a fracture. Weakened bone may also break during ordinary activities such as bending, lifting or even coughing. When the spine is involved, height is lost and a stooped posture develops. If the diet does not supply enough calcium the body takes it from bone, and sometimes bone loss occurs without any identifiable cause or simply runs in families.
causes: Oestrogen loss at the menopause
Ageing
Long-term steroid treatment
Low calcium and vitamin D, malabsorption
Overactive thyroid or parathyroid, low testosterone
Immobility
Chronic conditions and medicines other than steroids; sometimes no cause is found
riskFactors: Female sex, early menopause, or long gaps in sex-hormone exposure (including after removal of the ovaries or testes)
Thin bones running in the family
signs: Loss of height, stooped posture (kyphosis)
Fragility fracture after a fall from standing height
Fracture from an everyday stress such as bending, lifting or coughing
osteoporosis.diagnosis: DXA bone density scan (a T-score of −2.5 or lower), fracture risk calculators (FRAX), spine X-ray for vertebral fractures, and blood tests for vitamin D, calcium, thyroid and other secondary causes. Bone mineral density is measured non-invasively by DXA at the hip and spine, which NIAMS describes as the most reliable way to diagnose osteoporosis and predict fracture risk; a heel ultrasound can screen for bone loss but a DXA scan is still needed for the diagnosis. Clinicians also weigh fracture history, lifestyle, medical history and medicines, and may estimate future fracture risk with an online tool such as FRAX or QFracture. Screening is directed at older women and at younger women with additional risk factors.
osteoporosis.treatment: Calcium and vitamin D sufficiency, weight-bearing and balance exercise, fall prevention; bisphosphonates (alendronate) first line, denosumab or teriparatide for severe disease; treat secondary causes. Treatment combines lifestyle change (diet, exercise, fall prevention and cutting back on tobacco and alcohol) and calcium and vitamin D supplements with medication. Bisphosphonates are the main medicines used to prevent and treat osteoporosis in postmenopausal women; denosumab lessens bone loss and increases bone density. When osteoporosis comes from another condition or a medicine, the prescriber reviews the cause and whether the medicine is still needed (a medicine is never stopped or changed without their advice), and bone-protective treatment is often started at the same time.
osteoporosis.prevention: Build peak bone mass with exercise and calcium in youth, keep active, do not smoke, limit alcohol, ensure vitamin D, review medicines that cause falls or bone loss.
osteoporosis.seekCare: Any fracture from a minor fall after 50, sudden back pain in an older person, or loss of more than 4 cm in height should prompt assessment.

fracture.name: Bone fracture
fracture.definition: A break in the continuity of a bone, from a hairline crack to a shattered, displaced or open injury.
fracture.overview: Bones break when the force exceeds their strength: a fall on the outstretched hand fractures the wrist, a twist the ankle, a car crash the femur. In weakened bone (osteoporosis, cancer) a minor force is enough. Bone heals by forming a callus that is remodelled over months; the aim of treatment is to hold the fragments in a good position while it does. Symptoms vary with the bone involved: intense pain, a limb that looks out of place, swelling and tenderness, bruising and difficulty moving the part are typical, and some people feel a snap or grinding at the moment of injury. A simple crack may cause little pain, so a break is not always obvious. Healing takes weeks for minor fractures and months for severe ones, with the surrounding soft tissues often taking longer to recover than the bone itself; smoking and diabetes slow the process.
causes: Trauma: falls, sport, road accidents, assaults
Repeated stress (stress fractures in runners and soldiers)
Weakened bone: osteoporosis, tumours, infection
riskFactors: Poor balance, medicines that cause falls
signs: Pain, swelling, bruising, deformity
Inability to bear weight or use the limb
Crepitus
Open wound over the bone in open fractures
A snap or grinding sensation reported at the time of injury
Numbness or tingling below the injury, a warning sign of nerve or vessel damage
complications: Delayed healing, prolonged by smoking and diabetes
fracture.diagnosis: X-rays in two views; CT for complex joint, spine and pelvic fractures; MRI for occult fractures such as the scaphoid or stress fractures; assessment of circulation and nerves beyond the break. X-rays are the usual way to confirm a fracture and judge its position and severity, though it can be hard to tell clinically whether a bone is broken, so imaging is needed for most suspected breaks. CT shows the detail of complex joint, spine and pelvic fractures, and MRI shows soft tissues, bone bruising and stress fractures that X-rays miss.
fracture.treatment: Realign (reduce) if displaced, then hold: a cast or splint for stable fractures, or surgery with plates, screws, nails or external fixation for unstable ones. Pain relief, elevation, early movement of neighbouring joints, and physiotherapy. Open fractures need urgent cleaning and antibiotics. The common approach is immobilisation: a cast or splint keeps the bone from moving while it heals. Surgery is used when the bone needs realigning or holding, with metal rods, screws or plates securing the fragments. Open fractures, where the bone has broken the skin, need urgent surgery to remove debris, clean the wound and cut away unhealthy tissue, with antibiotics against infection. Pain relief and anti-inflammatory medicines are used, and physiotherapy afterwards restores movement, strength and function. Until help arrives, first aid is to keep the person still and calm, not to move the injured part or try to line up the bone, and to use ice and elevation for swelling.
fracture.prevention: Fall prevention and bone health in older adults, protective equipment in sport, road safety, treating osteoporosis. A balanced diet, hydration, avoiding smoking and heavy alcohol use, and following advice on when to bear weight support healing after a fracture.
fracture.seekCare: Emergency care for deformity, a bone through the skin, numbness or a cold pale limb, or a suspected hip, spine or pelvic fracture; same-day care for any inability to bear weight or use a limb after injury. Compartment syndrome, a rare but serious rise in pressure within the muscle compartments, most often develops in the first days after a fracture and causes sudden, intense pain and swelling; it needs emergency care. Redness, warmth, pus or fever around a wound suggest infection, particularly after an open fracture.

acl-injury.name: Anterior cruciate ligament injury
acl-injury.definition: A sprain or tear of the anterior cruciate ligament, the band inside the knee that stops the tibia sliding forward on the femur and controls rotation.
acl-injury.overview: ACL tears happen in a moment: a pivot, a sudden stop or a landing with the knee twisted inward, often with a pop and rapid swelling. The knee then gives way on turning. Young athletes, especially women, are most affected. Whether to reconstruct the ligament depends on the person's activity and instability. MedlinePlus describes the early picture: a popping sound or sensation at the moment of injury, obvious knee swelling within hours, pain that is worst when trying to put weight on the leg, an inability to carry on with the sport, and a feeling that the knee is unstable. Milder sprains may show up mainly as the knee giving way during use. Because the ligament is torn by a twisting load, the same force frequently damages the menisci, the joint cartilage or the collateral ligaments at the same time, which is why imaging looks beyond the ACL itself.

structures: Long head of right biceps femoris

causes: Non-contact pivoting, cutting or landing injuries (70%)
Direct blows to the knee
riskFactors: Poor landing mechanics and hip weakness
signs: A pop at injury, swelling within hours (haemarthrosis)
Positive Lachman and anterior drawer tests
Giving way on pivoting
Positive pivot-shift test (rotational instability)
acl-injury.diagnosis: History and examination are frequently enough to make the diagnosis: the twisting mechanism, the pop, the rapid haemarthrosis and a positive Lachman, anterior drawer or pivot-shift test. Plain X-rays cannot show ligaments but are taken to rule out a fracture. MRI is the reference investigation: it confirms the rupture and shows the meniscal, cartilage, collateral ligament and bone injuries that commonly accompany it and that change the treatment plan.
acl-injury.treatment: Immediate: rest, ice, compression, elevation and early physiotherapy. Structured rehabilitation restores function in many people; surgical reconstruction with a tendon graft (hamstring, patellar or quadriceps) is chosen for those with instability or pivoting sports, followed by 9 to 12 months of rehabilitation. NHS Scotland musculoskeletal guidance describes three broad pathways: rehabilitation as the first-line treatment, with reconstruction reserved for people who develop functional instability; reconstruction followed by post-operative rehabilitation as the first choice; or a period of pre-operative rehabilitation and then reconstruction. The choice depends on the person's age and sporting demands, the severity of the damage and the expected long-term outcome. The evidence comparing the routes is mixed: a review found only low-quality data, showing no clear difference in patient-reported knee function between surgical reconstruction and rehabilitation alone. Orthopaedic referral is advised where there is persistent subjective instability, recurrent giving way, ongoing mechanical symptoms such as locking, or failure to regain near-symmetrical strength and hop-test performance.
acl-injury.prevention: Neuromuscular training programmes (landing technique, hip and hamstring strength, balance) cut injury rates by half in athletes.
acl-injury.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a knee that swelled rapidly after a twisting injury, cannot straighten, locks or feels unstable. People are advised to avoid sport until the knee has been clinically assessed.

references.title: NHS Scotland Right Decisions (GGC MSK): Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL)

disc-herniation.name: Herniated (slipped) disc
disc-herniation.definition: Protrusion of the soft nucleus of an intervertebral disc through its fibrous outer ring, most often at the lower lumbar levels, which can press on a nerve root.
disc-herniation.overview: Discs weaken with age and can bulge or rupture under load. Most herniations cause back pain alone; when the extruded material compresses a nerve root the result is sciatica: sharp pain, tingling and numbness shooting down the leg in that root's territory, sometimes with weakness. Nine in ten settle within three months without surgery. The lower back is by far the commonest site, followed by the neck; herniations in the upper and mid back are rare. Injury or strain can push the disc out of place or break it open. Without pressure on a nerve the result may be a low backache or no pain at all; with nerve pressure, pain, numbness or weakness follow the path of the affected nerve, typically down one side. Sciatica is the name for this pattern of leg symptoms, not a diagnosis in itself: a herniated disc is its leading cause, but spinal stenosis, piriformis syndrome, pelvic injury or fracture, tumours and spondylolisthesis can produce the same picture.

structures: Intervertebral disk of fourth lumbar vertebra
Intervertebral disk of fifth lumbar vertebra
Intervertebral disk of fifth cervical vertebra

causes: Age-related disc degeneration
Lifting, twisting or a sudden strain
Repetitive loading
signs: Pain reproduced by straight-leg raising
Reduced ankle or knee reflex
Weak ankle dorsiflexion or big toe extension
Sensory loss in a dermatome
Pain, numbness or weakness following a single nerve's path down one leg
disc-herniation.diagnosis: Clinical, with MRI reserved for red flags, progressive neurological deficit or when surgery or injection is being considered, because disc bulges are common in people without symptoms. A plain spine X-ray cannot show the disc or confirm a herniation; MRI shows the disc, the nerve root and the degree of compression. Because other conditions, including nerve tumours, can mimic sciatica, imaging that does not match the clinical signs prompts a search for a non-disc cause.
disc-herniation.treatment: Stay active, pain relief (NSAIDs, short courses of stronger analgesia), physiotherapy, and time. Epidural steroid injections for severe radicular pain. Microdiscectomy for persistent sciatica beyond six to twelve weeks or for progressive weakness; emergency decompression for cauda equina syndrome. The first step is to stay active within comfort, with simple pain relief, followed by physiotherapy if symptoms persist; most people treated this way recover and return to normal activity. Anti-inflammatory medicines are used for mild to moderate pain, muscle relaxants for spasm, and short courses of stronger analgesia only when pain is severe and not responding. An epidural steroid injection is given under X-ray guidance so that the medicine reaches the exact level of the herniation. Surgery is considered when conservative treatment has not reduced the pain or when weakness progresses; only a minority of people with a symptomatic herniation need it.
disc-herniation.prevention: Lift with the legs, keep the back and core strong, healthy weight, do not smoke.
disc-herniation.seekCare: Emergency care for numbness around the saddle area, difficulty passing urine or controlling bowels, or weakness in both legs; urgent review for progressive weakness or unbearable pain.

gout.name: Gout
gout.definition: An inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of uric acid crystals in joints, triggered when blood urate is persistently high.
gout.overview: Uric acid is a waste product of purine metabolism. When its level exceeds saturation it crystallises in cool joints, classically the big toe, and the crystals provoke a sudden, exquisitely painful attack. Repeated attacks damage joints and form lumps (tophi). Lowering urate with medication dissolves the crystals and prevents attacks. Urate crystals can sit in a joint for a long time without causing symptoms; a flare is set off when something disturbs them, such as an infection, a joint injury, surgery, heavy drinking or certain foods. Flares typically bring intense pain, swelling and redness in one or more joints, last a week or two and then settle, and favour the joints furthest from the trunk: the toes, ankles, knees and fingers. Gout is several times commoner in men than in women. With early diagnosis, treatment and lifestyle changes, NIAMS describes it as one of the most controllable forms of arthritis.

structures: Proximal phalanx of right big toe

causes: Reduced kidney excretion of urate (90%)
Overproduction: high purine diet, cell breakdown, rare enzyme defects
riskFactors: Alcohol (beer and spirits), sugary drinks, red meat and shellfish
Acute illness, surgery or joint injury as triggers
signs: A red, hot, shiny, extremely tender joint, often the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Tophi on the ears, fingers and elbows in chronic gout
A flare that settles over a week or two, leaving a normal-looking joint between attacks
complications: Association with heart disease and kidney disease
gout.diagnosis: Crystals seen in joint fluid confirm it; a raised serum urate supports it (but may be normal during an attack); ultrasound or dual-energy CT shows crystal deposits. Infection must be excluded in a single hot joint. Gout is often diagnosed clinically from the history and examination. Aspirating fluid from the joint or bursa is the gold standard: the fluid is examined for urate crystals and tested for infection to exclude septic arthritis. Serum urate has limits: some people with gout have normal levels and many with high levels never develop gout, so clinicians may wait some weeks after a flare before measuring it.
gout.treatment: Attacks: NSAIDs, colchicine or steroids, started early; rest and ice. Prevention: allopurinol (or febuxostat) started after the attack settles and titrated to a target urate, with cover against flares for the first months; weight loss and diet changes. Treatment has two aims: easing the flare and preventing future flares and joint damage. Flares are treated with an NSAID such as ibuprofen, colchicine, or oral or injected corticosteroids, with paracetamol for additional pain relief. Where a medicine that raises urate is contributing, the prescriber may change it. Urate-lowering therapy is continued long term, because dissolving the crystals is what prevents further attacks and tophi; lifestyle changes such as losing weight, limiting alcohol and avoiding purine-rich foods support it.
gout.prevention: Healthy weight, limit alcohol and sugary drinks, moderate red meat and seafood, stay hydrated, review diuretics.
gout.seekCare: Same-day assessment for a hot swollen joint with fever, since septic arthritis looks identical and is an emergency. Joint fluid is tested for infection as well as crystals because septic arthritis can mimic gout.

type-1-diabetes.name: Type 1 diabetes
type-1-diabetes.definition: An autoimmune disease in which the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas are destroyed, so the body cannot regulate blood glucose without injected insulin.
type-1-diabetes.overview: Type 1 diabetes usually appears in childhood or young adulthood over days to weeks: thirst, frequent urination, weight loss and tiredness as glucose spills into the urine. Without insulin the body burns fat uncontrollably and produces acid (ketoacidosis), which is fatal untreated. Lifelong insulin replacement, increasingly with pumps and continuous glucose monitors, allows a full life. The NHS lists passing urine more than usual, especially at night, intense thirst, marked tiredness and unintended weight loss as the classic early signs, with blurred vision, fruity-smelling breath, slow-healing cuts and recurrent infections also possible; symptoms develop over a few days or weeks. Thirst and dehydration arise because the kidneys draw water from the body to clear excess glucose into the urine. Diabetic ketoacidosis is sometimes the first sign in someone not yet diagnosed: without insulin, ketones accumulate and make the blood acidic, and infection, injury, serious illness, missed insulin doses or the stress of surgery can tip someone with known diabetes into it.
causes: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells in genetically susceptible people, possibly triggered by viral infection
signs: Weight loss, dehydration
Ketone smell, deep sighing breathing and drowsiness in ketoacidosis
Blurred vision, slow-healing cuts and recurrent infections
Fruity-smelling breath
complications: Ketoacidosis triggered by infection, injury, serious illness, missed insulin or surgery
type-1-diabetes.diagnosis: Raised blood glucose with symptoms; ketones in blood or urine; antibodies (GAD, IA-2) and low C-peptide confirm type 1. HbA1c tracks control over months. Where a raised glucose is found in someone without symptoms, testing is repeated on a later day to confirm it. Autoantibody testing helps distinguish type 1 from other forms of diabetes, which is harder in children who are also obese.
type-1-diabetes.treatment: Insulin from diagnosis, as multiple daily injections (long-acting plus rapid-acting with meals) or a pump, matched to carbohydrate intake; glucose monitoring; structured education; annual screening of eyes, kidneys and feet; blood pressure and cholesterol control. Ketoacidosis is treated in hospital with insulin and fluids, and the underlying trigger, such as an infection, is treated at the same time. Early hypoglycaemia causes anxiety, sweating, hunger, tremor, palpitations and pallor; untreated it can progress to confusion, behavioural change, loss of consciousness, seizures and coma, which is why people on insulin and those around them are taught to recognise and treat it promptly.
type-1-diabetes.prevention: None yet, although immunotherapy can delay onset in high-risk relatives; good control lowers the risk of complications.
type-1-diabetes.seekCare: See a GP urgently, the same day for a child or young person, for increased thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness and weight loss: these can be the first signs of type 1 diabetes. Emergency care for vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, drowsiness or confusion in someone with diabetes, or for severe hypoglycaemia (confusion, seizure, unconsciousness). NHS advice is to call 999 or go to A&E if symptoms worsen quickly, or if the person becomes sleepy or confused or starts breathing faster and deeper than usual.

references.title: NHS: Symptoms of type 1 diabetes and how it's diagnosed
NCBI PMC: Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Children and Adolescents; Diagnostic and Therapeutic Pitfalls

type-2-diabetes.name: Type 2 diabetes
type-2-diabetes.definition: A metabolic disease in which the body's cells respond poorly to insulin (insulin resistance) and the pancreas gradually fails to compensate, leaving blood glucose persistently high.
type-2-diabetes.overview: Type 2 diabetes accounts for over 90% of diabetes and is closely tied to excess weight and inactivity, though genes matter greatly. It develops silently over years; many people are diagnosed on a routine test or when a complication appears. Sustained weight loss early on can put it into remission.
causes: Insulin resistance from visceral fat and inactivity, plus progressive beta-cell failure, on a strong genetic background
riskFactors: Age over 40 (younger in South Asian, Black and Hispanic populations)
signs: Often none
Central obesity, acanthosis nigricans
Reduced foot sensation and pulses in established disease
Retinal changes
type-2-diabetes.diagnosis: HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or more, or fasting glucose of 7 mmol/L or more, repeated if without symptoms. Annual checks of kidney function, urine albumin, eyes, feet, blood pressure and lipids.
type-2-diabetes.treatment: Diet, weight loss and activity are the foundation; metformin first, then SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists, DPP-4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas or insulin as needed; statins and blood pressure treatment reduce cardiovascular risk; structured education and foot care.
type-2-diabetes.prevention: Diet and exercise programmes halve the risk in people with prediabetes; keeping a healthy weight and staying active are the key measures.
type-2-diabetes.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain, or for drowsiness or confusion with very high glucose readings. Get same-day advice from a GP or NHS 111 for a foot wound that is red, hot or discharging, or sudden vision change.

hypothyroidism.name: Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
hypothyroidism.definition: Insufficient thyroid hormone, most often because the immune system destroys the thyroid gland, slowing the body's metabolism.
hypothyroidism.overview: Thyroxine sets the pace of nearly every cell, so its lack slows everything: energy, thought, bowel, heart rate and heat production. Symptoms creep in over months and are easily mistaken for ageing or depression. A simple blood test makes the diagnosis and a daily tablet of levothyroxine restores normal life. Symptoms are non-specific and gradual: difficulty concentrating, low mood, hair loss, a hoarse voice and heavier or irregular periods are common additions to tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation and dry skin. No single symptom reliably identifies the condition, and many people with mild (subclinical) hypothyroidism have no symptoms at all, so attributing a given complaint to the thyroid can be difficult. Hashimoto's disease, in which the immune system attacks the thyroid, is the most common cause where iodine intake is adequate; iodine deficiency remains the commonest cause worldwide.
causes: Autoimmune (Hashimoto's) thyroiditis
Treatment of an overactive thyroid (radioiodine, surgery)
Iodine deficiency worldwide
Drugs: amiodarone, lithium, immunotherapy
Pituitary failure (rare)
Congenital
Thyroiditis (inflammation of the gland)
Radiotherapy to the neck
signs: Weight gain, dry skin and hair, puffy face
Slow pulse, cold intolerance
Slow-relaxing reflexes
Goitre
Hoarse voice, constipation, heavy periods
Enlarged thyroid felt on examination of the neck
Muscle weakness, aches and cramps
complications: Premature birth and other pregnancy complications when untreated
Rarely, muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) or fluid around the heart in severe untreated disease
hypothyroidism.diagnosis: A raised TSH with a low free T4 confirms primary hypothyroidism; thyroid peroxidase antibodies indicate the autoimmune cause. Cholesterol is often raised. A GP typically asks about symptoms, examines the neck for an enlarged thyroid and arranges blood tests. Because hypothyroidism contributes to high cholesterol, people found to have raised cholesterol are tested for it. Routine screening of adults without symptoms is debated: the US Preventive Services Task Force found insufficient evidence for it, whereas the American Thyroid Association recommends periodic screening of people at higher risk.
hypothyroidism.treatment: Levothyroxine once daily on an empty stomach, dose adjusted by TSH every six to eight weeks until stable, then checked yearly; higher doses are needed in pregnancy. Dosing starts low and rises gradually, with regular blood tests until the right dose is found; some people feel better within weeks, others take months, and treatment is usually lifelong. Side effects such as sweating, chest pain, headaches and sleep problems mostly occur when the dose is too high. Extra care is needed in people with heart conditions, diabetes or adrenal problems. People who are mildly affected with few or no symptoms may not need treatment and are simply monitored. An unusually high dose requirement prompts a check for absorption problems, missed doses or coeliac disease.
hypothyroidism.prevention: Adequate iodine intake; screening in pregnancy and after thyroid treatment. Pregnant women taking levothyroxine usually need more frequent testing, and the dose often changes.
hypothyroidism.seekCare: See a doctor for persistent tiredness with weight gain, cold intolerance or low mood; emergency care for drowsiness, very low temperature or confusion in someone with known hypothyroidism. Myxoedema coma, an extreme form in which the body's functions slow to a life-threatening point, needs immediate hospital treatment.

hyperthyroidism.name: Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
hyperthyroidism.definition: Excess thyroid hormone, most often from Graves' disease, in which antibodies stimulate the thyroid to overproduce.
hyperthyroidism.overview: Too much thyroxine speeds the body up: weight loss despite appetite, tremor, palpitations, sweating, anxiety and diarrhoea. Graves' disease can also inflame the eye muscles, pushing the eyes forward. Treatment blocks hormone production, destroys thyroid tissue with radioiodine, or removes the gland. Thyroid hormones regulate how the body uses energy, so an excess touches nearly every organ, including the rhythm of the heart. Older adults may present differently, with loss of appetite or withdrawal from people rather than restlessness, and the condition is sometimes mistaken for depression or dementia. Thyroid eye disease (Graves' ophthalmopathy), with dryness, redness, protrusion or double vision, affects a minority of people whose overactive thyroid is due to Graves' disease. The course depends on the cause: thyroiditis may settle without treatment as stored hormone is used up, whereas Graves' disease usually worsens over time if left untreated.
causes: Graves' disease (autoimmune, 75%)
Toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma
Thyroiditis releasing stored hormone
Excess thyroxine tablets, amiodarone, iodine loads
Thyroiditis following a viral infection, some medicines or pregnancy
Rarely, a non-cancerous pituitary tumour; iodine contrast dye mainly matters when the thyroid already has a problem
signs: Fast pulse, atrial fibrillation, tremor, warm moist skin
Goitre, sometimes with a bruit
Eye signs: lid retraction, protrusion, double vision
Weight loss, brisk reflexes
In older adults: apathy, loss of appetite and withdrawal rather than overactivity
complications: Thyroid eye disease with vision loss
Underactive thyroid after radioiodine or surgery, needing lifelong levothyroxine
hyperthyroidism.diagnosis: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 or T3; TSH-receptor antibodies confirm Graves'; a radioiodine uptake scan distinguishes causes when antibodies are negative. Assessment starts with the history and a blood test of thyroid function. If the blood test confirms overactivity, further tests identify the cause, because the cause determines treatment. The diagnosis is usually prompted by unexplained weight loss, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or persistent nervousness and tiredness.
hyperthyroidism.treatment: Beta blockers for symptoms; antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, propylthiouracil) for 12 to 18 months; radioiodine or thyroidectomy for relapse or large goitres, followed by levothyroxine replacement. Eye disease needs specialist care and stopping smoking. Antithyroid medicines reduce hormone production; radioactive iodine destroys thyroid cells; surgery removes part or all of the gland; and beta blockers such as propranolol ease a rapid heartbeat while definitive treatment takes effect. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid later, which then needs lifelong hormone replacement.
hyperthyroidism.prevention: Not smoking reduces eye disease; no prevention for the autoimmune process itself.
hyperthyroidism.seekCare: Urgent care for palpitations with breathlessness or chest pain, fever with confusion and agitation, or sudden vision change or eye pain. NHS and NIDDK advice is to see a GP for unexplained weight loss, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or persistent nervousness and tiredness, since untreated hyperthyroidism can cause serious heart problems.

urinary-tract-infection.name: Urinary tract infection
urinary-tract-infection.definition: Bacterial infection of the bladder (cystitis) or, when it ascends, the kidney (pyelonephritis), usually by gut bacteria such as Escherichia coli.
urinary-tract-infection.overview: UTIs are among the commonest bacterial infections, far more frequent in women because the short urethra lets bacteria reach the bladder easily. Cystitis burns and nags but is rarely dangerous; kidney infection causes fever, loin pain and vomiting and can lead to sepsis, especially in the elderly, in pregnancy and with obstruction. Infection begins when bacteria enter the urethra and move upwards to the bladder (cystitis) and sometimes on to the kidneys (pyelonephritis); E. coli is the main agent, and other bacteria, viruses or fungi are rare causes. Presentation varies with age: infants often have fever, irritability or poor feeding, while older adults may have no urinary symptoms and instead show confusion resembling dementia, marked fatigue or incontinence. UTI is the most common hospital-acquired infection, and most of those cases are associated with urinary catheters. Resistance to antibiotics is an increasing problem in treating UTI.
causes: Gut bacteria (E. coli in 80%) ascending the urethra
Catheters and instrumentation
Obstruction: stones, enlarged prostate
riskFactors: Female anatomy (a short urethra close to the vagina and anus), sexual activity, spermicides
Incomplete bladder emptying, kidney stones, prostate enlargement
signs: Suprapubic tenderness
Loin tenderness and fever in pyelonephritis
Confusion in older adults
Cloudy or bloody urine
In infants: fever, irritability and reduced feeding
In older adults: dementia-like confusion, fatigue or new incontinence without urinary complaints
complications: Recurrent infection, defined as repeated episodes within a few months
urinary-tract-infection.diagnosis: Symptoms and a urine dipstick (nitrites, leucocytes, blood) in uncomplicated cystitis; urine culture in men, children, pregnancy, recurrent or complicated infection; blood tests and imaging if kidney infection or obstruction is suspected. Diagnosis combines clinical assessment with a urinalysis and, where indicated, a urine culture, which usually takes several days to complete; audits of general practice have found that prescribing antibiotics without any urine testing is common and is a recognised area for improvement.
urinary-tract-infection.treatment: A short course of antibiotics (nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim for cystitis; longer courses of a broader agent for kidney infection), fluids and pain relief. Intravenous antibiotics for severe infection; relief of any obstruction. Cystitis often gets better by itself, and UK services may issue a delayed ('back-up') antibiotic prescription to be started only if symptoms do not settle. Paracetamol eases the discomfort. Complicated infection may need a longer course or intravenous antibiotics, and persistent symptoms warrant further testing rather than repeated empirical courses.
urinary-tract-infection.prevention: Fluids, emptying the bladder after sex, avoiding spermicides, vaginal oestrogen after the menopause, prophylactic antibiotics or methenamine for frequent recurrences. NHS advice also includes avoiding perfumed bubble bath, soap or talcum powder around the genitals, preferring showers to baths, passing urine as soon as the urge is felt and wiping from front to back; for some women with recurrent cystitis a single antibiotic dose taken within an hour of sex is prescribed.
urinary-tract-infection.seekCare: Urgent care for fever, shivering, loin pain, vomiting or confusion with urinary symptoms, symptoms in pregnancy or in a man, or blood in the urine that persists.

references.title: NCBI PMC: Urinary Tract Infections: Prevention, Diagnosis, and Treatment
NHS Cornwall and Isles of Scilly ICB: Urinary tract infections

kidney-stones.name: Kidney stones
kidney-stones.definition: Hard crystals, most commonly calcium oxalate, that form in the kidney and can pass into and block the ureter.
kidney-stones.overview: Stones form when urine is concentrated and rich in stone-forming salts. A stone leaving the kidney scrapes and blocks the ureter, producing renal colic: waves of agonising pain from the loin to the groin with blood in the urine. Most stones under 5 mm pass on their own; larger or infected obstructions need intervention. Stones form when urine carries high concentrations of calcium, oxalate or phosphate, although in many individuals no specific reason is ever found. Many small stones cause no symptoms and are passed unnoticed. Pain that comes in waves and radiates from the back or side towards the groin usually means a stone has moved into the ureter; blood in the urine, nausea and vomiting and pain on passing urine are common, and fever or chills point to infection alongside the stone, which changes the urgency entirely.
causes: Low urine volume
High urinary calcium, oxalate or uric acid
Urinary infection with urease-producing bacteria (struvite stones)
Rare inherited causes (cystinuria)
Metabolic conditions such as hyperparathyroidism that raise urinary calcium
riskFactors: High salt, animal protein and oxalate intake
Vigorous exercise or a hot environment without replacing fluid
A first stone at a young age
signs: Restless, unable to lie still
Loin tenderness
Blood in the urine on dipstick
Fever if infected
complications: Recurrence in half within ten years
Acute kidney injury with reduced urine output when drainage is blocked
kidney-stones.diagnosis: Non-contrast CT of the urinary tract is the definitive test; ultrasound in pregnancy and children; urine dipstick and culture, kidney function and calcium and urate levels; analysis of the passed stone. Assessment begins with the history, including existing conditions, current medicines, diet and whether relatives have had stones, and with examination. Blood tests check calcium, phosphate, uric acid and electrolytes; urinalysis looks for crystals and red blood cells. Ultrasound is often the first imaging used to estimate stone size and check for obstruction, with plain X-ray or non-contrast CT as alternatives; CT is the usual choice for severe pain in adults.
kidney-stones.treatment: Strong analgesia (NSAIDs are most effective), fluids, and drugs to relax the ureter to help small stones pass; shock-wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy with laser fragmentation or percutaneous surgery for larger stones; urgent drainage with a stent or nephrostomy if obstructed and infected. Stone size is the main determinant of initial treatment, and around eight in ten stones pass spontaneously. Alpha blockers and calcium-channel blockers can aid passage by relaxing the ureter. Stones unlikely to pass are candidates for minimally invasive treatment such as shock-wave lithotripsy. For adults with recurrent calcium oxalate stones and high urinary calcium, NICE CKS advises considering a thiazide once salt intake has been reduced; potassium citrate and allopurinol are used for other recurrent stone types.
kidney-stones.prevention: Drink enough to pass 2 to 2.5 litres of urine a day, limit salt and animal protein, keep normal calcium intake, lemon juice for citrate; specific drugs for recurrent formers. Recurrence is common, approaching half of people within ten years, which is why fluid intake, dietary review and, for repeated stones, metabolic assessment with targeted medication are emphasised.
kidney-stones.seekCare: Emergency care for colicky pain with fever or shivering, vomiting preventing fluids, pain not controlled by painkillers, or a single functioning kidney. NHS advice is to ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for severe pain or for fever and chills. Unrelieved pain, reduced urine output, infection or acute kidney failure in the presence of an obstructing stone are medical emergencies.

references.title: NIDDK: Symptoms & Causes of Kidney Stones
NICE CKS: Renal or ureteric colic - acute

chronic-kidney-disease.name: Chronic kidney disease
chronic-kidney-disease.definition: Persistent reduction in kidney function (a filtration rate below 60 ml/min) or evidence of kidney damage such as protein in the urine, for more than three months.
chronic-kidney-disease.overview: The kidneys lose nephrons slowly and silently, most often from diabetes and high blood pressure. Symptoms appear only when function is severely reduced, so CKD is found by blood and urine tests in at-risk people. Progression can be slowed for years; a minority reach kidney failure needing dialysis or transplantation. Chronic kidney disease means the kidneys are damaged or structurally abnormal and cannot filter blood as they should, with function declining over months to years. Because early disease causes no symptoms, NHS guidance recommends testing for people with high blood pressure, diabetes or a family history of kidney disease. When symptoms do appear in advanced disease they are non-specific: tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands from fluid retention, shortness of breath, nausea, loss of appetite and blood in the urine, all of which overlap with many less serious conditions. An episode of acute kidney injury can also leave lasting damage that becomes CKD.
causes: Diabetes
High blood pressure
Glomerulonephritis
Polycystic kidney disease
Obstruction (prostate, stones)
Recurrent infection, drugs (NSAIDs, lithium), reflux
Acute kidney injury that does not fully recover
riskFactors: Black, South Asian and Indigenous ancestry
signs: High blood pressure
Oedema
Pallor from anaemia
Late: itching, muscle twitching, drowsiness
Blood in the urine
complications: Cardiovascular disease (the leading cause of death in CKD)
Low calcium and high phosphate levels
chronic-kidney-disease.diagnosis: Estimated GFR from blood creatinine and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, repeated over three months; the two together both make the diagnosis and set its severity, staged G1 to G5 by filtration rate and A1 to A3 by albuminuria. Albumin is a protein that passes into the urine when the filtering units are damaged, so it is an early marker even while the eGFR is still normal. Testing is the only reliable way to know how well the kidneys are working, which is why at-risk groups are screened rather than waiting for symptoms. Ultrasound of the kidneys shows size, obstruction and cysts, and further tests look for the cause, because the cause changes management.
chronic-kidney-disease.treatment: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, statins, glucose control, salt restriction, stopping smoking, avoiding NSAIDs, dose adjustment of medicines; treating anaemia and bone disease; preparing for dialysis or transplantation as function declines. CKD cannot be cured, but progression can often be slowed for years. NIDDK describes blood pressure control as the most important single step; ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the usual choice because they also reduce protein leak, and loop diuretics manage fluid. Blood glucose and cholesterol are treated alongside. Lifestyle measures include lower-salt food, limiting alcohol, staying physically active and not smoking. Anaemia, bone and mineral disorder and fluid overload are treated as they arise. When function falls far enough (kidney failure), dialysis or a kidney transplant is needed for survival, and preparation begins well in advance.
chronic-kidney-disease.prevention: Control diabetes and blood pressure, keep a healthy weight, do not smoke, avoid regular NSAIDs, stay hydrated during illness, have kidney checks if at risk. People with diabetes, high blood pressure or a family history of kidney disease are offered regular eGFR and urine albumin checks so that damage is found early.
chronic-kidney-disease.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness, chest pain, severe drowsiness, or a sudden fall in urine output; routine review for swelling, frothy urine or persistently high blood pressure. CKD is usually found by routine testing rather than symptoms, so people in at-risk groups are advised to ask about kidney checks.

references.title: NIDDK: Chronic Kidney Disease Tests & Diagnosis

anaemia.name: Anaemia
anaemia.definition: A haemoglobin concentration below normal (roughly under 130 g/L in men and 120 g/L in women), reducing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.
anaemia.overview: Anaemia is a sign, not a diagnosis. Iron deficiency from blood loss or poor intake is the commonest cause worldwide; others include vitamin B12 and folate deficiency, chronic disease, kidney failure, inherited haemoglobin disorders and bone marrow failure. Finding the cause matters because in adults it can be bleeding from a bowel cancer. Haemoglobin inside red cells carries oxygen, so a low concentration leaves tissues short of oxygen and the heart working harder to compensate. How much a person notices depends largely on how quickly the anaemia develops: a slow fall from chronic blood loss may cause few symptoms until it is marked, whereas a rapid fall is felt early. Iron deficiency arises when more blood and iron are lost than the body can replace, when iron is poorly absorbed (as in coeliac disease or Crohn's disease), when the diet is low in iron, or when needs rise, as in pregnancy and breastfeeding. Mild or moderate iron deficiency may produce no symptoms at all and is often picked up on a routine blood count.
causes: Iron deficiency: heavy periods, gut bleeding, poor diet, malabsorption, pregnancy
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Chronic inflammation or kidney disease
Thalassaemia and sickle cell disease
Haemolysis
Bone marrow disease
Malabsorption from coeliac disease or Crohn's disease
Increased requirement in pregnancy and breastfeeding
signs: Pale conjunctivae and palms
Fast pulse, flow murmur
Spoon nails, sore tongue in iron deficiency
Jaundice in haemolysis
Numb feet and unsteadiness in B12 deficiency
Reported cravings for non-food items (pica), hair loss, headache or tinnitus in iron deficiency
anaemia.diagnosis: Full blood count is the starting point: a low haemoglobin with a reduced mean cell volume (MCV) is the usual first finding in iron deficiency, and red cell size separates the main groups of cause. Serum ferritin reflects iron stores and confirms iron deficiency; B12, folate, reticulocytes and a blood film narrow down other causes. Because anaemia is a sign rather than a diagnosis, the search for the cause matters as much as the count: coeliac tests, and endoscopy or colonoscopy to look for a bleeding source in men and in women past the menopause. A bone marrow examination is reserved for cases where the diagnosis remains unclear after these tests. During treatment, blood tests are repeated every few months to confirm that the haemoglobin is rising.
anaemia.treatment: Treat the cause; oral iron for three months after correction (or intravenous iron if not tolerated), B12 injections or folate, erythropoietin in kidney disease, transfusion only for severe or symptomatic anaemia. Oral iron tablets are the standard first step and are usually effective; they commonly cause gastrointestinal side effects, and taking them with meals eases this at the cost of reduced absorption. Treatment continues for about three months after the haemoglobin has returned to normal so that iron stores are replenished, with follow-up blood tests to check the response. Intravenous iron is used when tablets are not tolerated or not absorbed. Correcting the count without finding and treating the cause leaves the problem to recur.
anaemia.prevention: Iron-rich diet with vitamin C, treating heavy periods, iron supplements in pregnancy where advised, avoiding unnecessary NSAIDs. Groups at higher risk, such as women with heavy periods, pregnant women, people on restricted diets and older people, benefit from attention to dietary iron and early testing when symptoms appear.
anaemia.seekCare: Urgent care for breathlessness at rest, chest pain, fainting, or black or bloody stools; routine review for persistent tiredness and pallor. NHS guidance is that anyone with symptoms of anaemia should see their GP, who can usually diagnose it with a simple blood test; untreated iron deficiency can lead to heart problems, complications in pregnancy and delayed development in children.

sepsis.name: Sepsis
sepsis.definition: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated body response to infection.
sepsis.overview: Any infection can trigger sepsis, most often pneumonia, urinary infection, abdominal infection or skin infection. The immune response spills over into the whole body: blood vessels leak and dilate, clotting is disturbed, and organs fail. Sepsis kills millions a year; each hour of delay in antibiotics raises mortality, so recognition is everything.
causes: Bacterial infection most often (pneumococcus, E. coli, staphylococci, streptococci, meningococcus)
Viral, fungal or parasitic infections
riskFactors: Weak immune system: chemotherapy, steroids, diabetes, no spleen
Pregnancy and the weeks after birth
signs: Fast breathing (over 22/min), fast pulse, low blood pressure
New confusion or drowsiness
Mottled, cold or clammy skin; non-blanching rash
Passing little urine
Very high or abnormally low temperature
complications: Acute kidney injury, lung failure, liver failure
sepsis.diagnosis: Clinical recognition (NEWS or qSOFA scores), blood cultures and cultures from the likely source before antibiotics, lactate, blood counts, kidney and liver function, clotting; imaging to find the source.
sepsis.treatment: The 'sepsis six' within an hour: oxygen, blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics, intravenous fluids, lactate measurement and urine output monitoring; then source control (drain an abscess, remove an infected line), vasopressors and organ support in intensive care.
sepsis.prevention: Vaccination, hand hygiene, prompt treatment of infections, careful care of wounds and catheters, and knowing the warning signs.
sepsis.seekCare: Call emergency services for an infection with slurred speech or confusion, extreme shivering or muscle pain, passing no urine in a day, severe breathlessness, mottled or discoloured skin, or a feeling of impending doom; for children also fast breathing, a fit, blue or pale skin, a non-fading rash, or unusual drowsiness.

breast-cancer.name: Breast cancer
breast-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour arising from the cells that line the ducts or lobules of the breast. It may remain within the ducts (in situ) or invade the surrounding tissue and spread to the axillary lymph nodes and beyond.
breast-cancer.overview: Breast cancer is the commonest cancer in women worldwide, and most cases occur after 50. Most tumours start in the milk ducts, fewer in the milk-producing lobules; ductal carcinoma in situ stays within the duct, while invasive cancer has broken through it. Every invasive cancer is tested for oestrogen receptors, progesterone receptors and the HER2 protein, which with grade and stage decides treatment. It is rare in men, and anyone with breast tissue can develop it.

structures: Sternocostal part of left pectoralis major
Sternocostal part of right pectoralis major

causes: Accumulated DNA damage in duct or lobule cells, driven in part by lifetime exposure to oestrogen and progesterone
Inherited faults in BRCA1, BRCA2 and a few other genes, responsible for a minority of cases
Previous radiotherapy to the chest, particularly in youth
No single cause is found in most cases; ageing is the strongest factor
riskFactors: Increasing age: most cases are diagnosed after 50
A close relative with breast or ovarian cancer, or a known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation
Longer lifetime oestrogen exposure: an early first period, a late menopause, no pregnancies or a first pregnancy late in life
Combined hormone replacement therapy and, to a small degree, the combined contraceptive pill: the increase is small, relates to how long they are used, and falls after stopping
Alcohol, and being overweight after the menopause
Dense breast tissue on mammography, a previous breast cancer or some benign breast conditions

In trans women, several years of feminising hormone therapy: the risk is thought to be higher than in cis men but lower than in cis women; in men, conditions that raise oestrogen levels such as obesity, Klinefelter syndrome and cirrhosis
signs: A firm, irregular, usually painless lump in the breast or armpit
Dimpling, puckering or an orange-peel texture of the skin over the breast
A newly inverted nipple, a rash or crusting on the nipple, or blood-stained discharge
A change in the size or outline of one breast
In advanced disease, bone pain, breathlessness or jaundice from spread to bone, lung or liver
complications: Spread to the axillary lymph nodes and to bone, lung, liver or brain (metastatic breast cancer)
Lymphoedema of the arm after axillary surgery or radiotherapy
Bone loss and menopausal symptoms from endocrine therapy; heart effects of some chemotherapy and HER2-targeted drugs
Recurrence in the breast, chest wall or elsewhere, sometimes many years later
Anxiety, altered body image and loss of fertility in younger patients
breast-cancer.diagnosis: A suspicious lump or nipple change is assessed in a one-stop breast clinic by triple assessment: clinical examination, imaging (mammography, with ultrasound for younger women and dense breasts) and a core needle biopsy of anything abnormal. The biopsy confirms invasive or in situ disease, grade and receptor status (oestrogen receptor, progesterone receptor and HER2). Ultrasound of the axilla with needle sampling of suspicious nodes, and MRI in selected cases, complete local staging; CT and bone scans are reserved for larger tumours, involved nodes or symptoms suggesting spread. Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 is offered when the age at diagnosis, tumour type or family history suggests an inherited cause. Screening in England invites women, and anyone else registered female with a GP who has breast tissue, for mammography every three years; the first invitation arrives between the ages of 50 and 53, routine invitations stop after 70, and anyone aged 71 or over can still ask their local breast screening service for screening. Trans women who have taken hormones for some years and trans men who have not had chest surgery may need to ask to be included.
breast-cancer.treatment: Early breast cancer is treated with surgery: either wide local excision, removing the tumour with a margin of normal tissue and followed by radiotherapy to the rest of the breast, or mastectomy, in each case with sentinel lymph node biopsy to check the axilla and clearance of the nodes if they are involved. Reconstruction can be immediate or delayed. Treatment given after surgery, or before it to shrink a large tumour, is chosen by receptor status and the risk of recurrence: chemotherapy; endocrine therapy for oestrogen-receptor-positive cancers (tamoxifen, or an aromatase inhibitor after the menopause), taken for years; and trastuzumab or similar antibodies for HER2-positive disease. Metastatic breast cancer is not usually curable but is often controlled for years with endocrine, targeted and chemotherapy, radiotherapy for painful bone deposits and bone-protecting drugs. Care is planned by a multidisciplinary team following NICE guidance.
breast-cancer.prevention: Not all breast cancer can be prevented, but keeping to a healthy weight, being physically active, limiting alcohol and breastfeeding all lower the risk, and hormone replacement therapy is best reviewed regularly and continued only for as long as it is needed. Attending screening finds cancers before they can be felt. People at high risk because of family history or a BRCA mutation can be offered earlier and more frequent imaging, risk-reducing medicines or risk-reducing surgery, planned with a genetics service.
breast-cancer.seekCare: See a GP promptly about any new lump in the breast or armpit, skin dimpling, a change in a nipple or blood-stained nipple discharge, in anyone with breast tissue, at any age and whatever their gender. Chest masculinisation removes most but not all of the breast tissue, so a new lump or change in the chest wall still needs the same assessment. NICE recommends urgent referral to a breast clinic for an unexplained breast lump in anyone aged 30 or over and for discharge, retraction or other changes of one nipple in anyone aged 50 or over. A hot, red, swollen breast with fever suggests infection and should be seen the same day; a red, inflamed breast that does not settle with antibiotics also needs referral.

cervical-cancer.name: Cervical cancer
aliases: squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
cervical-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour of the cervix, the neck of the uterus, that develops almost always from persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV) after years of precancerous change.
cervical-cancer.overview: Cervical cancer arises at the transformation zone, where the lining of the cervical canal meets that of the outer cervix. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV, mainly types 16 and 18, turns the cells there abnormal (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN). Most infections clear and most CIN regresses, but some progresses to invasive cancer over years, which is why screening can find and treat the change first. It affects anyone with a cervix, including trans men and non-binary people.
causes: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, mainly types 16 and 18, passed on by skin-to-skin sexual contact
Viral proteins that disable the cell's tumour-suppressor controls, so that abnormal cells (CIN) accumulate further mutations over years
A very small number of cervical cancers are not associated with HPV
riskFactors: Not being vaccinated against HPV and not attending cervical screening
Smoking, which makes it more likely that an HPV infection persists and progresses
A weakened immune system: HIV infection, organ transplant or long-term immunosuppressive medicines
Earlier first sexual intercourse and a greater number of sexual partners, because these increase exposure to HPV
Long-term use of the combined contraceptive pill (a small increase that falls after stopping)
A previous high-grade abnormality (CIN) or another HPV-related cancer
signs: Often none: precancer and early cancer are usually found only by screening
Bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, or periods that become heavier
A persistent, unusual or smelly vaginal discharge, and pain or discomfort during sex
On examination, an abnormal-looking cervix that bleeds on contact; a hard, irregular mass in advanced disease
In advanced disease, swelling of a leg, blood in the urine or symptoms of kidney obstruction where the tumour blocks a ureter
complications: Spread to the vagina, parametrium, bladder, rectum and pelvic lymph nodes, and later to lung, liver and bone
Blockage of one or both ureters causing hydronephrosis and kidney failure
Fistulas between the bladder or rectum and the vagina, from tumour or from radiotherapy
Loss of fertility after radical surgery or chemoradiotherapy, and early menopause where the ovaries are removed or damaged by radiotherapy; a higher chance of preterm birth after cone biopsy or LLETZ
Long-term bowel, bladder and sexual effects of pelvic radiotherapy
cervical-cancer.diagnosis: Screening detects HPV and abnormal cells before cancer develops: a sample of cells from the transformation zone is tested first for high-risk HPV and, if positive, examined under the microscope, and abnormal results lead to colposcopy. Symptoms such as unusual bleeding are investigated by speculum examination of the cervix and referral for colposcopy, not by a screening test. At colposcopy the cervix is examined under magnification after acetic acid is applied, and a biopsy or a loop excision (LLETZ) provides tissue for the pathologist. If cancer is confirmed, staging uses examination, MRI of the pelvis, CT of the chest and abdomen and sometimes PET-CT, with blood tests including kidney function; the extent of spread (the FIGO stage) determines treatment.
cervical-cancer.treatment: Precancerous change (CIN) is treated by removing or destroying the transformation zone, usually with a large loop excision (LLETZ) under local anaesthetic or with a cone biopsy, after which HPV testing continues as a test of cure. Very early cancers can be removed by cone biopsy or, for those who wish to preserve fertility, by trachelectomy, which removes the cervix and upper vagina and leaves the uterus in place. Most early-stage cancers are treated by radical hysterectomy with removal of the pelvic lymph nodes, or by radiotherapy where surgery is unsuitable. Locally advanced disease is treated with chemoradiotherapy: external beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy to the cervix, with weekly platinum chemotherapy to sensitise the tumour. Cancer that has spread or returned is treated with chemotherapy, sometimes with targeted or immunotherapy drugs, and with palliative care to control symptoms.
cervical-cancer.prevention: Two measures prevent most cervical cancer. HPV vaccination, offered in the UK to all children aged 12 to 13 and to some adults at higher risk, protects against the types that cause the great majority of cases and works best before exposure to the virus. It does not protect against every high-risk type, so everyone with a cervix still needs cervical screening even if they have been vaccinated. Cervical screening is offered in England to everyone with a cervix aged 25 to 64, including trans men and non-binary people (who may need to ask their GP practice if they are registered as male), at intervals that depend on age and the HPV result; it finds and treats precancer before it becomes cancer. Not smoking, and using condoms, which reduce but do not remove HPV transmission, also help. The WHO strategy for eliminating cervical cancer combines high coverage of vaccination, screening and treatment of precancer and cancer.
cervical-cancer.seekCare: See a GP about bleeding between periods, after sex or after the menopause, a persistent unusual discharge, or pelvic pain. These are usually not cancer, but they need an examination and cannot be assessed by a screening test. Any bleeding after the menopause needs prompt assessment. NICE advises an urgent suspected cancer referral for post-menopausal bleeding in anyone aged 55 or over, mainly to rule out cancer of the womb lining, and bleeding below that age is still investigated. NICE also advises considering an urgent suspected cancer referral when the appearance of the cervix on examination is consistent with cervical cancer. Attend screening when invited, and ask to be included if you have a cervix but have not been invited.

ectopic-pregnancy.name: Ectopic pregnancy
ectopic-pregnancy.definition: A pregnancy in which the fertilised egg implants and begins to grow outside the cavity of the uterus, most often in a fallopian tube, where it cannot develop normally and can rupture the tissue around it.
ectopic-pregnancy.overview: After fertilisation in the ampulla of the fallopian tube, the embryo normally travels into the uterus and implants in the endometrium about a week later. In an ectopic pregnancy it implants elsewhere: most often in the tube itself, less commonly in the interstitial part of the tube where it enters the uterus, in the cervix, an ovary, a previous caesarean scar or the abdominal cavity. The NHS estimates that around 1 in every 90 pregnancies in the UK is ectopic. Symptoms usually appear between about the fourth and twelfth week of pregnancy, often in the first weeks after a missed period and sometimes before the pregnancy is known. The tube cannot stretch or support a placenta, so as the pregnancy grows it bleeds and can tear through the tubal wall, causing heavy bleeding into the abdomen. An ectopic pregnancy cannot be moved into the uterus and cannot survive, and a ruptured ectopic pregnancy is a life-threatening emergency. It can occur in anyone who can become pregnant, including trans men and non-binary people with a uterus and tubes, and should be considered in anyone of reproductive age with pelvic pain or bleeding until pregnancy has been excluded.
causes: Implantation of the fertilised egg outside the uterine cavity, usually because damage or narrowing of the fallopian tube slows or blocks the embryo's passage to the uterus
Scarring of the tube after pelvic inflammatory disease, most often from chlamydia or gonorrhoea
Previous surgery on the tubes, including sterilisation and its reversal, and a previous ectopic pregnancy
Impaired movement of the tube and its cilia, which smoking and hormonal factors are thought to affect
In many cases no cause is found
riskFactors: Pelvic inflammatory disease or a history of sexually transmitted infection
Surgery on the fallopian tubes, including sterilisation, or other pelvic or abdominal surgery

Becoming pregnant with an intrauterine device or system in place, or while taking the progestogen-only pill: these methods make pregnancy itself unlikely, but a pregnancy that does happen is more likely to be ectopic
signs: Tenderness, sometimes with guarding, in one side of the lower abdomen
Tenderness on moving the cervix or beside the uterus on pelvic examination, sometimes with a tender mass
Pain in the tip of the shoulder, from blood in the abdomen irritating the diaphragm, which points to internal bleeding
Pallor, a fast pulse, low blood pressure and collapse when the tube has ruptured
Vaginal bleeding that is often lighter, darker and more watery than a period
complications: Rupture of the tube with heavy bleeding into the abdomen, shock and, if not treated quickly, death
Loss of the affected fallopian tube, or damage to it after surgery that keeps the tube
Reduced fertility and a higher chance of another ectopic pregnancy in a later pregnancy
Persistent trophoblast tissue after salpingotomy or medical treatment, needing further treatment
Rhesus sensitisation in a rhesus-negative woman if anti-D is not given after surgery
Grief and anxiety about future pregnancies; the loss is a bereavement as well as an emergency
ectopic-pregnancy.diagnosis: Ectopic pregnancy is suspected in anyone who could be pregnant and has lower abdominal or pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding or unexplained faintness, so a pregnancy test comes first. If it is positive, a transvaginal ultrasound scan in an early pregnancy unit looks for a pregnancy inside the uterus; it may instead show a mass beside the ovary, occasionally with a heartbeat, or free fluid behind the uterus that indicates bleeding. When neither an intrauterine nor an ectopic pregnancy is seen, the situation is called a pregnancy of unknown location: serum hCG is measured and repeated 48 hours later, when a rise of about two thirds or more over 48 hours makes a developing pregnancy in the uterus more likely, though it does not exclude an ectopic and a scan is still arranged; a falling level suggests a pregnancy that is failing, and a slow rise or a plateau raises suspicion of an ectopic. NICE advises interpreting the result alongside the clinical picture rather than on its own. A full blood count and the blood group are checked, and miscarriage, a bleeding or twisted ovarian cyst, appendicitis and urinary infection are considered. Anyone who is shocked or in severe pain is treated as having a rupture without waiting for further tests.
ectopic-pregnancy.treatment: Treatment follows NICE guidance and depends on how unwell the person is, the size of the ectopic pregnancy and the hCG level. Expectant management, with repeated hCG measurements until the level falls to normal, suits a small unruptured ectopic pregnancy with a low and falling hCG in someone who has little or no pain and can return for follow-up. Medical treatment is an injection of methotrexate, which stops the trophoblast cells dividing so that the pregnancy is reabsorbed; blood tests continue until hCG is undetectable, and pregnancy is avoided for some months afterwards as the team advises. Surgery, almost always laparoscopic, is used for significant pain, a larger mass, a high hCG, a visible heartbeat or rupture: salpingectomy removes the affected tube, while salpingotomy keeps a tube when the other one is damaged, at the cost of residual tissue that needs further monitoring. Rupture is an emergency treated with resuscitation, transfusion if needed and immediate surgery, and rhesus-negative women who have surgery are offered anti-D immunoglobulin. The loss is a bereavement as well as an emergency, and most women conceive again, even after a tube has been removed.
ectopic-pregnancy.prevention: Most ectopic pregnancies cannot be prevented, but the risk can be lowered by reducing the chance of tubal damage: using condoms to protect against chlamydia and other sexually transmitted infections, being tested and treated promptly if infection is suspected, and not smoking. Anyone who has had an ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery or pelvic inflammatory disease should tell their GP or midwife as soon as they know they are pregnant so that an early scan can confirm that the pregnancy is in the uterus.
ectopic-pregnancy.seekCare: Anyone who could be pregnant and has one-sided lower abdominal or pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding or brown watery discharge, or pain in the tip of the shoulder should contact a GP, NHS 111 or an early pregnancy unit the same day, even if no period has been missed yet. Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden severe abdominal pain, feeling faint or collapsing, a racing pulse, or looking very pale and feeling sick and sweaty with pain, as these can mean the tube has ruptured and internal bleeding has started.

endometriosis.name: Endometriosis
endometriosis.definition: A chronic condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus (the endometrium) grows outside the uterus, most often on the ovaries, the peritoneum and the ligaments of the pelvis, where it responds to the hormones of the menstrual cycle and causes inflammation, pain and scarring.
endometriosis.overview: Endometriosis affects roughly 1 in 10 women of reproductive age worldwide, and anyone with a uterus and ovaries can develop it, including trans men and non-binary people. The misplaced tissue bleeds a little with each period but has no way out, so it provokes inflammation, adhesions and cysts: a deposit on the ovary can grow into a blood-filled endometrioma, often called a chocolate cyst, and deep infiltrating disease can involve the uterosacral ligaments, the space between the rectum and the vagina, the bowel and the bladder. The result is period pain that stops normal life, pain with sex, bowel and bladder symptoms and, for some, difficulty conceiving. The condition depends on oestrogen, so it begins after puberty and symptoms usually improve after the menopause, although they do not always settle, and oestrogen-containing HRT can keep deposits active. Its symptoms overlap with other pelvic conditions and examination and scans are often normal in early disease, and the NHS notes that getting a diagnosis can take a long time.
causes: The cause is not fully understood, and endometriosis probably arises in more than one way
Retrograde menstruation, in which menstrual blood carrying endometrial cells flows back along the fallopian tubes into the pelvis, is the most widely accepted explanation
Transformation of peritoneal cells into endometrial-like tissue, and spread of cells through lymph or blood vessels, may explain deposits at distant sites
Oestrogen drives the deposits to grow and bleed, and an altered immune response fails to clear them
Genetic factors: the condition runs in families
riskFactors: A mother or sister with endometriosis
Early first period, short cycles, and heavy or prolonged periods
Never having given birth, or a late first pregnancy
Anything that obstructs the outflow of menstrual blood, such as a congenital abnormality of the uterus or vagina
Reproductive age: the condition is rare before puberty, and symptoms usually improve after the menopause, although they do not always settle
signs: Tenderness on pelvic examination, particularly behind the uterus and over the uterosacral ligaments
Nodules felt in the posterior vaginal fornix in deep disease
A fixed, retroverted uterus, or an enlarged ovary where an endometrioma has formed
A normal examination, which does not rule endometriosis out
complications: Subfertility and infertility, from adhesions that distort the tubes and ovaries and from inflammation that impairs fertilisation and implantation
Chronic pelvic pain with a large effect on work, education, relationships and mental health
Ovarian endometriomas, which can rupture or twist the ovary (torsion)
Adhesions binding the bowel, bladder and uterus together; rarely bowel obstruction or blockage of a ureter
A small increase in the risk of some types of ovarian cancer, although the overall risk remains low
endometriosis.diagnosis: Diagnosis starts with the pattern of symptoms: pain that follows the menstrual cycle, pain during or after sex, and cyclical bowel or urinary symptoms, together with an abdominal and pelvic examination. Transvaginal ultrasound is the first investigation and can show endometriomas and deep deposits in the bowel or bladder, but it often misses superficial disease on the peritoneum. MRI helps to map deep infiltrating disease before surgery. Laparoscopy, with a biopsy of the deposits seen, is the definitive test, although NICE advises that a normal examination, ultrasound or MRI should not be used to rule the condition out or to withhold treatment. There is no diagnostic blood test. A pregnancy test, urinalysis and a full blood count help to exclude pregnancy, urine infection and anaemia while the cause of pelvic pain is being worked out.
endometriosis.treatment: Treatment depends on symptoms, age and whether pregnancy is wanted. Pain is managed first with paracetamol and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen. Hormonal treatment aims to stop the deposits responding to the cycle: the combined hormonal contraceptive or a progestogen is offered first, and GnRH analogues, which produce a temporary menopause, are reserved for specialist use and are normally given with add-back hormone therapy to protect bone and limit menopausal symptoms. Some of these treatments, such as the combined hormonal contraceptive and contraceptive progestogens, also prevent pregnancy; others, including GnRH analogues, are not contraceptives, so contraception is discussed separately. Hormonal treatment does not have a lasting effect on fertility once it is stopped. Surgery is laparoscopic excision or ablation of the visible deposits, removal of endometriomas and division of adhesions; deep disease involving the bowel, bladder or ureter is managed by a specialist endometriosis centre. Hysterectomy, with or without removal of the ovaries, is a last resort for those who have completed their family; it is normally combined with excision of the deposits, it does not guarantee that pain will end, and hormone replacement therapy is discussed if the ovaries are removed before the menopause. Fertility treatment, pain management services and support groups such as Endometriosis UK are part of long-term care.
endometriosis.prevention: There is no known way to prevent endometriosis. Hormonal contraception that makes periods lighter or stops them may reduce symptoms and slow the growth of deposits. Recognising the symptoms early, and taking period pain that disrupts life seriously rather than accepting it as normal, shortens the delay to diagnosis and treatment.
endometriosis.seekCare: See a GP for period pain that stops normal activities, pain during or after sex, pain when passing urine or opening the bowels during a period, blood in the urine or stool during periods, or difficulty getting pregnant. Seek urgent care for sudden severe pelvic pain, pain with fever or vomiting, fainting, or pain with a positive pregnancy test, which can signal a ruptured or twisted cyst or an ectopic pregnancy.
