fibroids.name: Fibroids
fibroids.definition: Benign (non-cancerous) growths of smooth muscle and fibrous tissue that develop in the muscular wall of the uterus, ranging from the size of a pea to a mass that fills the abdomen.
fibroids.overview: Fibroids are the commonest benign (non-cancerous) growth of the uterus: the NHS estimates that around 1 in 3 women develop them at some point, most often between the ages of 30 and 50, and they are more common in Black women. They occur in anyone with a uterus, including trans men and non-binary people. Fibroids depend on oestrogen and progesterone, so they grow during the reproductive years and in pregnancy and usually shrink after the menopause. They are described by position: intramural fibroids sit within the myometrium, subserosal fibroids bulge from the outer surface towards the abdomen, submucosal fibroids push into the cavity and distort the lining, and pedunculated fibroids hang on a stalk inside or outside the uterus. Many cause no symptoms and are found by chance on a scan. When they do cause trouble it is usually heavy periods, pressure on the bladder or bowel, pain or, with submucosal fibroids, difficulty conceiving.
causes: The exact cause is unknown; each fibroid arises from a single smooth muscle cell of the myometrium that multiplies abnormally
Growth is driven by oestrogen and progesterone, which is why fibroids appear after puberty, enlarge in pregnancy and shrink after the menopause
Genetic changes within the fibroid cells and local growth factors sustain the growth
Fibroids are not caused by infection and do not develop from the endometrium
riskFactors: A mother or sister with fibroids
Being overweight, which raises oestrogen levels
Never having given birth; pregnancy appears to lower the risk
signs: An enlarged, firm, irregular uterus felt on abdominal or pelvic examination
A mass in the lower abdomen that can be large enough to resemble pregnancy
Pallor and other signs of iron deficiency anaemia from heavy bleeding
A normal examination when the fibroids are small
complications: Iron deficiency anaemia from heavy or prolonged periods
Pressure effects: frequent urination or difficulty emptying the bladder, constipation, and rarely blockage of a ureter
Subfertility and miscarriage, particularly with submucosal fibroids that distort the cavity
Problems in pregnancy: pain from degeneration of a fibroid, an awkward position of the baby, obstructed labour, caesarean birth and heavier bleeding after delivery
Torsion of a pedunculated fibroid, causing sudden severe pain

Uterine sarcoma (leiomyosarcoma) is a rare cancer that can look like a fibroid on a scan; fibroids themselves are not thought to turn cancerous, but a fibroid that grows quickly, or any growth or bleeding after the menopause, needs prompt assessment
fibroids.diagnosis: Fibroids are often discovered on a scan done for another reason. When symptoms prompt investigation, the history covers the heaviness and pattern of bleeding, pressure symptoms and plans for pregnancy, and the examination feels for an enlarged or irregular uterus. Ultrasound, transvaginal or through the abdomen, is the first imaging and shows the number, size and position of the fibroids; NICE recommends it when the uterus can be felt through the abdomen or a pelvic mass is suspected. MRI maps fibroids more precisely before myomectomy or uterine artery embolisation and helps to distinguish them from adenomyosis. Hysteroscopy is used when submucosal fibroids are suspected and allows small ones to be removed at the same time. A full blood count is offered to anyone with heavy bleeding to check for anaemia; NICE does not recommend testing ferritin routinely, and iron treatment is guided by the blood count and symptoms. A pregnancy test is done in anyone of reproductive age with bleeding or a pelvic mass.
fibroids.treatment: Fibroids that cause no symptoms need no treatment, only review if they are large. For heavy bleeding the options are those for heavy menstrual bleeding generally. For fibroids smaller than about 3 cm, NICE advises the levonorgestrel intrauterine system as the first option where the cavity is not distorted, with tranexamic acid, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory such as ibuprofen, the combined pill or cyclical progestogens if it is unsuitable, and iron to correct anaemia. Fibroids of 3 cm or more are referred for specialist assessment. GnRH analogues shrink fibroids and stop bleeding by inducing a temporary menopause; they are used for a few months before surgery, with add-back hormone therapy to protect bone. Procedures that keep the uterus are myomectomy (removal of the fibroids through the abdomen, laparoscopically or hysteroscopically), uterine artery embolisation, in which a radiologist blocks the blood supply so that the fibroids shrink, endometrial ablation for small fibroids with heavy bleeding, and MRI-guided focused ultrasound where it is available. The effect of uterine artery embolisation and myomectomy on future pregnancy is uncertain and is discussed before choosing between them; endometrial ablation is not suitable for anyone who may want a pregnancy. Hysterectomy is the definitive treatment for those who have completed their family and whose symptoms are severe.
fibroids.prevention: There is no proven way to prevent fibroids. Keeping to a healthy weight may lower the risk. Treating heavy periods early prevents iron deficiency anaemia, and regular review of known fibroids catches growth or new symptoms before they cause complications.
fibroids.seekCare: See a GP for periods heavy enough to disrupt life, bleeding between periods, tiredness or breathlessness that could mean anaemia, pressure symptoms in the bladder or bowel, a swelling in the lower abdomen, or difficulty conceiving. Seek urgent care for sudden severe abdominal pain, bleeding that soaks a pad every hour for several hours, or faintness. Any bleeding after the menopause, or a fibroid that grows after the menopause, needs prompt assessment.

gender-dysphoria.name: Gender dysphoria (gender incongruence)
gender-dysphoria.definition: The distress that can arise when a person's gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth. The mismatch itself is called gender incongruence and is not an illness.
gender-dysphoria.overview: Gender identity is a person's inner sense of being a man, a woman, both, neither or another gender; when it does not match the sex recorded at birth, the unease can be intense and lasting, though many trans and non-binary people have little or no dysphoria. The WHO's ICD-11 lists gender incongruence under conditions related to sexual health and not among mental or behavioural disorders. Support, social transition, hormones and surgery can relieve dysphoria for those who want them; lack of support, care and acceptance is associated with worse mental health.
causes: The origin of gender identity is not fully understood; biological and developmental influences are studied but no single cause is established
There is no evidence that it is caused by parenting or family circumstances, and gender identity is not a choice
Distress arises from the mismatch between identity and the body's sex characteristics, and from how others respond: misgendering, rejection and discrimination
Rarely, gender incongruence occurs alongside a difference of sex development, but most people with gender dysphoria have typical chromosomes and hormones
riskFactors: Puberty, when secondary sexual characteristics that do not match identity develop
Rejection by family or peers, bullying, harassment and discrimination
Long waits for specialist assessment and care
Co-existing depression or anxiety, which deepen the distress
Isolation from other trans people and from reliable information and support
signs: Persistent discomfort with the body's primary or secondary sex characteristics, or with being treated as the assigned gender
A strong and lasting wish to live as, and be recognised in, the experienced gender, often expressed through name, pronouns, clothing and social role
Low mood, anxiety, poor sleep, fatigue, social withdrawal or self-neglect accompanying the distress
Steps taken to change appearance, such as binding, tucking, padding or choice of clothing and hair
complications: Depression, anxiety, self-harm and raised suicide risk, especially with rejection, discrimination or long delays in care
Social isolation and leaving education or work
Harm from unregulated hormones bought online and used without monitoring
Reduced fertility on hormone therapy, which may not be fully reversible, and permanent loss of fertility after removal of the gonads, if eggs or sperm were not stored beforehand
Treatment risks that need monitoring: venous thromboembolism on oestrogen, a raised red cell count on testosterone, bone loss after gonadectomy if hormones are interrupted
gender-dysphoria.diagnosis: There is no test for gender identity. Assessment by a specialist gender service, usually after GP referral, covers how gender identity has developed, the distress it causes, physical and mental health, and what the person hopes for. ICD-11 describes gender incongruence as a marked and persistent incongruence between experienced gender and assigned sex; the DSM-5-TR diagnosis of gender dysphoria asks for incongruence lasting at least six months with clinically significant distress or impairment, whereas ICD-11 gender incongruence does not require distress and is classified outside the mental disorders. The blood tests linked from this page are used to monitor hormone therapy and general health, not to diagnose gender incongruence.
gender-dysphoria.treatment: Care aims to help people live comfortably in their gender; the mix is individual, and some want none of it. It can include psychological support, social transition (name, pronouns, clothing, documents), voice and communication therapy, hair removal, gender-affirming hormone therapy (oestradiol with a testosterone-suppressing medicine, usually stopped once the testes are removed, for trans women and some non-binary people; testosterone for trans men and some non-binary people) prescribed and monitored by a specialist team, and genital, chest, breast and facial surgery. Hormones and gonadal surgery reduce fertility, so storing sperm or eggs is discussed first. Care for under-18s is provided by specialist services, and policies differ between countries and have changed: in England, puberty blockers for gender incongruence are available only through specialist research pathways, and prescribing outside those pathways is restricted.
gender-dysphoria.prevention: Gender incongruence is not something to prevent or cure. What can be prevented is the harm that comes with it: acceptance and support from family, school and workplace, prompt access to assessment and care, respectful use of the person's name and pronouns, mental health support when needed, and protection from bullying and discrimination all reduce distress and the risk of self-harm.
gender-dysphoria.seekCare: Ask a GP for referral to a gender service if gender-related distress is persistent or affecting daily life. Seek urgent help from emergency services or a crisis line for thoughts of suicide or self-harm. Tell a doctor about any hormones taken without a prescription so that monitoring can be arranged. Anyone on hormone therapy with a swollen painful leg, chest pain or sudden breathlessness needs urgent assessment for a clot.

ovarian-cancer.name: Ovarian cancer
ovarian-cancer.definition: A malignant tumour of the ovary or, as is now recognised for many cases of the commonest type, of the adjacent fallopian tube, which spreads early across the peritoneal surfaces of the pelvis and abdomen.
ovarian-cancer.overview: The ovaries sit deep in the pelvis and early disease causes only vague symptoms such as bloating and feeling full, so most ovarian cancers are diagnosed only after they have spread across the peritoneum. Risk rises with age, and there is no screening programme, so recognising persistent new symptoms is the main route to earlier diagnosis. Trans men and non-binary people who have not had their ovaries removed can develop ovarian cancer and need the same assessment of persistent symptoms.
causes: Accumulated genetic damage in the epithelium of the fallopian tube or ovarian surface; repeated ovulation and the repair it demands are thought to contribute, which is why factors that suppress ovulation are protective
Inherited mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2, or in the mismatch-repair genes of Lynch syndrome, in a minority of cases
Endometriosis, from which clear cell and endometrioid cancers can arise
No identifiable cause in most cases
riskFactors: Increasing age: most cases occur after the menopause
A family history of ovarian or breast cancer, or a known BRCA1, BRCA2 or Lynch syndrome mutation
Never having been pregnant, infertility, and an early first period or late menopause
Hormone replacement therapy (a small increase while it is taken)
Being overweight, and smoking (linked to some subtypes)
signs: Persistent bloating or a visibly swollen abdomen, rather than bloating that comes and goes
Feeling full quickly or losing appetite, with unexplained weight loss, or weight gain from fluid
Pelvic or abdominal pain, needing to pass urine urgently or more often, and a change in bowel habit
A pelvic or abdominal mass, ascites or a pleural effusion on examination in advanced disease
In younger women with germ cell or hormone-producing tumours, a rapidly enlarging mass, abnormal bleeding or signs of hormone excess
complications: Spread across the peritoneum, omentum and bowel surface with ascites; later to lymph nodes, liver, lung and pleura
Bowel obstruction from tumour deposits, a common problem in advanced disease
Torsion or rupture of a large ovarian tumour, causing sudden severe pain
Venous thromboembolism, which is frequent with ovarian cancer and its treatment
Surgical menopause and loss of fertility after removal of both ovaries; chemotherapy side effects including nerve damage and low blood counts
Recurrence, which is common after treatment of advanced disease
ovarian-cancer.diagnosis: NICE guidance directs GPs to measure serum CA125 in women, and in anyone else with ovaries, who reports persistent abdominal distension (bloating), feeling full or loss of appetite, pelvic or abdominal pain, or increased urinary urgency or frequency on a persistent or frequent basis, particularly more than 12 times a month, and especially if they are aged 50 or over, or who develops symptoms resembling irritable bowel syndrome for the first time after 50. If CA125 is raised, an ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis follows, and the ultrasound findings, menopausal status and CA125 level are combined into a risk of malignancy index that guides referral to a specialist gynaecological cancer team. In women under 40, alpha-fetoprotein and hCG are also measured because germ cell tumours are more likely. CT of the abdomen and pelvis assesses spread, and the diagnosis is confirmed on tissue, either from an image-guided biopsy of a peritoneal deposit or from the fluid of ascites, or at surgery. Genetic testing for BRCA1, BRCA2 and Lynch syndrome is offered to people diagnosed with epithelial ovarian cancer and, when a mutation is found, to their relatives. CA125 is not a reliable test for early disease: it can be normal in early cancer and raised in endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic infection, pregnancy and other conditions.
ovarian-cancer.treatment: Treatment combines surgery and chemotherapy, planned by a specialist multidisciplinary team according to stage and subtype. Surgery for epithelial cancer usually removes the uterus, both ovaries and tubes and the omentum, samples or removes lymph nodes and aims to clear all visible tumour from the peritoneum (cytoreductive or debulking surgery); when disease is extensive, chemotherapy may be given first and surgery performed once the tumour has shrunk. Young women with early-stage disease can sometimes keep the uterus and the other ovary. Platinum-based chemotherapy (carboplatin, usually with paclitaxel) is given after surgery for all but the earliest stages. Maintenance treatment with a PARP inhibitor after chemotherapy prolongs remission, particularly in cancers with BRCA mutations or related DNA-repair defects, and bevacizumab is used in some advanced cases. Germ cell tumours respond very well to chemotherapy and are often cured with fertility preserved. Recurrent disease is treated with further chemotherapy, sometimes further surgery, and symptom control including drainage of ascites.
ovarian-cancer.prevention: No screening test has been shown to reduce deaths from ovarian cancer, so there is no population screening programme. Risk is lower in women who have used the combined contraceptive pill, been pregnant or breastfed, and after tubal ligation or hysterectomy, and keeping to a healthy weight and not smoking also help. Women with a strong family history should be referred to a genetics service: carriers of BRCA1, BRCA2 or Lynch syndrome mutations can be offered risk-reducing removal of the tubes and ovaries once their family is complete, which greatly lowers the risk, with attention afterwards to the effects of surgical menopause.
ovarian-cancer.seekCare: See a GP if bloating, feeling full quickly, pelvic or abdominal pain or needing to pass urine more often are new, persistent or frequent and unexplained, especially after the age of 50. These symptoms are far more often due to something else, but they warrant a CA125 blood test and, if it is raised, an ultrasound. Bowel symptoms resembling irritable bowel syndrome that appear for the first time after 50, and unexplained weight loss, fatigue or a change in bowel habit, warrant the same assessment, and any abdominal or pelvic swelling or lump that can be felt should be examined without delay. Seek urgent care for sudden severe abdominal pain, vomiting with a swollen abdomen and no bowel movements, or a painful swollen leg or breathlessness, which may indicate torsion, bowel obstruction or a clot.

pelvic-organ-prolapse.name: Pelvic organ prolapse
pelvic-organ-prolapse.definition: Descent of one or more of the pelvic organs (the bladder, uterus, rectum, small bowel or, after hysterectomy, the top of the vagina) from their normal position so that they bulge into, and sometimes out of, the vagina, because the pelvic floor muscles and connective tissue that support them have weakened or stretched.
pelvic-organ-prolapse.overview: The pelvic organs are held in place by the levator ani muscles of the pelvic floor, the endopelvic fascia and the ligaments that anchor the cervix and upper vagina to the pelvic walls. When these supports are torn or stretched, most often by childbirth, or weaken with age and the fall in oestrogen after the menopause, the organs sag under the pressure of the abdomen and the vaginal walls fold inwards. Prolapse is named for the compartment involved: an anterior wall prolapse (cystocele) carries the bladder, a posterior wall prolapse (rectocele) the rectum, an enterocele a loop of small bowel, a uterine prolapse brings the cervix down the vagina, and a vault prolapse is descent of the top of the vagina after hysterectomy. It is staged from 1, a slight descent within the vagina, to 4, in which the organ lies entirely outside the vaginal opening. Some degree of prolapse is found on examination in many women who have given birth, though far fewer have symptoms, and it is rarely dangerous: symptoms range from a mild sense of heaviness to a visible bulge that interferes with passing urine, opening the bowels and sex. It affects anyone with a vagina and pelvic floor, including trans men and non-binary people.
causes: Stretching and tearing of the pelvic floor muscles, fascia and nerves during pregnancy and vaginal birth, especially with a large baby, a long second stage of labour, a forceps or ventouse delivery or several births
Weakening of the supporting tissues with age and after the menopause, when oestrogen levels fall
A long-term rise in pressure inside the abdomen from obesity, a chronic cough, constipation and straining, or repeated heavy lifting
Loss of the uterus and its ligaments after hysterectomy, which leaves the vaginal vault less well supported
Inherited weakness of connective tissue, including joint hypermobility syndromes
riskFactors: Vaginal births, particularly a large baby, an instrumental delivery or a long labour
Chronic constipation, a long-term cough or heavy manual work
A family history of prolapse or a connective tissue disorder
signs: A bulge of the vaginal wall or the cervix seen at the vaginal opening on straining or standing, or protruding at rest in advanced prolapse
Descent of the anterior or posterior vaginal wall on speculum examination, recorded by stage
Weak pelvic floor muscle contraction on examination
Ulceration, thickening or bleeding of the exposed vaginal skin in a prolapse that sits outside the body
Leakage of urine on coughing, or a residual volume of urine after voiding
complications: Urinary problems: stress incontinence, difficulty emptying the bladder, recurrent urinary tract infections and, rarely, kinking of the ureters with back-pressure on the kidneys in severe prolapse
Bowel problems: constipation and incomplete emptying, sometimes needing the vaginal wall to be pressed back to open the bowels
Ulceration, discharge and bleeding of the exposed vaginal skin, and rarely a prolapse that cannot be pushed back
Discomfort or loss of confidence during sex
Pessary problems such as discharge, vaginal irritation or ulceration if it is not checked and changed regularly
Recurrence of prolapse after surgery, or new stress incontinence once the bulge no longer kinks the urethra
pelvic-organ-prolapse.diagnosis: The history covers the sensation of a bulge or dragging, urinary and bowel symptoms, sexual function and how much the prolapse affects daily life; NICE recommends using a validated pelvic floor symptom questionnaire. Examination with a speculum, at rest and while straining and sometimes standing, shows which compartment is affected and how far it descends, and is recorded using a standard staging system such as the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system. The strength of the pelvic floor muscles is assessed at the same time. A urine dipstick is done if there are urinary symptoms, and a bladder scan measures the residual volume if emptying seems incomplete. Imaging is not usually needed: ultrasound or MRI is reserved for unusual symptoms, suspected other pelvic disease or, in advanced prolapse, to check the kidneys for back-pressure. A prolapse found by chance in someone without symptoms does not need treatment.
pelvic-organ-prolapse.treatment: Treatment is chosen according to the symptoms, the stage of prolapse, wishes about future pregnancy and sexual activity, and general health; NICE NG123 sets out the options. Lifestyle measures come first: losing weight if overweight, treating constipation and cough, and avoiding heavy lifting. NICE advises considering a supervised programme of pelvic floor muscle training for at least 16 weeks as a first option for symptomatic POP-Q stage 1 or stage 2 prolapse, and it improves symptoms in many women. Vaginal oestrogen is considered when there are signs of vaginal atrophy after the menopause. A vaginal pessary, a silicone or plastic ring or shelf that holds the prolapse up, is an option for symptomatic prolapse at any stage, used on its own or alongside pelvic floor muscle training, and is often chosen by those who prefer to avoid surgery or are not fit for it; it is checked, cleaned or changed by a clinician at regular intervals agreed with the service. Surgery is considered when other measures have not helped: repair of the vaginal wall using the woman's own tissue, vaginal hysterectomy or a uterus-preserving operation such as sacrohysteropexy, and sacrocolpopexy or sacrospinous fixation for vault prolapse. NICE restricts synthetic mesh inserted through the vagina, and any mesh procedure needs a full discussion of risks and benefits and recording in a national registry. Continence surgery is sometimes combined with the repair when stress incontinence is also present.
pelvic-organ-prolapse.prevention: Pelvic floor muscle training during pregnancy and after childbirth, continued as a lifelong habit, is the main preventive measure and also reduces urinary incontinence. Keeping to a healthy weight, avoiding constipation with a high-fibre diet and enough fluid, treating a chronic cough, stopping smoking and lifting safely all lower the strain on the pelvic floor. Vaginal oestrogen does not prevent prolapse, but treating vaginal dryness and thinning after the menopause can ease symptoms and is offered alongside other measures.
pelvic-organ-prolapse.seekCare: See a GP, or ask for a referral to a pelvic health physiotherapist or urogynaecology clinic, for a feeling of heaviness or a bulge in the vagina, a lump at the vaginal opening, difficulty passing urine or opening the bowels, urinary leakage or discomfort during sex; these problems are common and treatable and do not have to be accepted as part of ageing. Seek prompt care if a prolapse becomes stuck outside the body and cannot be pushed back, if it bleeds or is painful, if you cannot pass urine, or if you have fever, loin pain or repeated urinary infections.

polycystic-ovary-syndrome.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.definition: A common hormonal condition in which the ovaries make more androgens (hormones such as testosterone, which everyone makes, usually in higher amounts in men) than usual and release eggs irregularly or not at all, often with many small immature follicles visible on the ovaries.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.overview: Polycystic ovary syndrome is one of the commonest endocrine conditions in women of reproductive age, affecting about 1 in 10 women in the UK, and anyone with ovaries can have it, including trans men and non-binary people. The name misleads: the so-called cysts are small follicles that have stalled before ovulation rather than true cysts, and some people with the syndrome have normal-looking ovaries. Insulin resistance is central. High insulin levels push the ovaries to make androgens and lower the liver's output of sex hormone-binding globulin, so more testosterone is free to act. The excess androgen disrupts the maturing of follicles and causes acne and excess hair, while irregular ovulation leads to infrequent periods and subfertility. PCOS is also a metabolic condition, with a raised long-term risk of type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and abnormal blood lipids, and it is linked with low mood and sleep apnoea. Features usually begin in the late teens or early twenties and vary widely in severity from one person to another.
causes: The exact cause is unknown; PCOS is thought to result from a combination of genetic and environmental factors

Insulin resistance: the body's cells respond poorly to insulin, so more is produced, and the high insulin level stimulates the ovaries to make androgens and lowers the liver's output of sex hormone-binding globulin, raising free testosterone
Altered signalling from the pituitary, with relatively high luteinising hormone (LH), which further drives androgen production by the ovary
Excess androgen stops follicles maturing to ovulation, so they accumulate as small follicles around the edge of the ovary
Family history: PCOS and type 2 diabetes cluster in families
riskFactors: A mother or sister with PCOS
Being overweight or gaining weight, which worsens insulin resistance and symptoms but does not cause the condition on its own
Reproductive age: features usually appear in the years after puberty
signs: Hirsutism: coarse, dark hair on the face, chest, abdomen or back in a male pattern
Acne and oily skin, and thinning of scalp hair in a male pattern
Acanthosis nigricans: dark, velvety thickening of the skin of the neck, armpits and groin, a marker of insulin resistance
Raised body weight, particularly around the waist
Enlarged ovaries with many small follicles on ultrasound
complications: Type 2 diabetes, and gestational diabetes in pregnancy
Raised cardiovascular risk: high blood pressure, abnormal cholesterol and central weight gain

Thickening of the lining of the uterus (endometrial hyperplasia) and, over years, endometrial cancer, because infrequent periods leave the lining exposed to oestrogen without the regular shedding that progesterone brings
Subfertility from irregular or absent ovulation, and a higher risk of miscarriage and complications in pregnancy
Obstructive sleep apnoea, fatty liver disease, depression and anxiety
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.diagnosis: PCOS is diagnosed on the Rotterdam criteria when two of three features are present and other causes have been excluded: infrequent or absent ovulation, shown by irregular or absent periods; clinical or biochemical signs of excess androgen, meaning hirsutism, acne or a raised testosterone or free androgen index on blood tests; and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. Ultrasound is unnecessary if the first two are present, and it is not used to make the diagnosis in adolescents, in whom ovaries with many follicles are normal. Blood tests measure testosterone, sex hormone-binding globulin, LH and FSH, and check prolactin and thyroid function, because thyroid disease, a raised prolactin, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome and androgen-secreting tumours can mimic the syndrome; a very high testosterone level or rapid virilisation points to a tumour rather than PCOS. Once the diagnosis is made, blood glucose or HbA1c, a lipid profile, blood pressure and weight are checked and then reviewed regularly.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.treatment: There is no cure, so treatment is matched to the symptoms that matter most to the person and to the long-term risks. Weight loss where weight is raised, and regular exercise, improve insulin resistance, ovulation and androgen symptoms and are the foundation of care. The combined hormonal contraceptive pill regulates bleeding and reduces acne and hirsutism; if it is unsuitable, a cyclical progestogen is used to bring on a regular withdrawal bleed, or a hormonal intrauterine system is used to keep the lining thin; either protects the endometrium in anyone who has only a few periods a year. Periods that are infrequent do not mean pregnancy is impossible, so contraception is still needed if pregnancy is not wanted. Metformin can improve insulin resistance and cycle regularity and is used in some people, usually alongside lifestyle change. For fertility, ovulation is induced with letrozole or clomifene under specialist care, with metformin, laparoscopic ovarian drilling or IVF as further options. Excess hair is managed with hair removal, eflornithine cream or, under specialist advice, an anti-androgen, and acne is treated in the usual ways. Screening for diabetes and cardiovascular risk continues lifelong, and mood and sleep problems are asked about and treated.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.prevention: PCOS cannot be prevented, but its complications largely can. Keeping to a healthy weight, staying active and eating well reduce insulin resistance and the risk of diabetes and heart disease; regular checks of blood glucose, blood pressure and lipids pick up problems early; and making sure the lining of the uterus is shed regularly, whether by natural periods or a progestogen, protects against endometrial cancer.
polycystic-ovary-syndrome.seekCare: See a GP for periods that are infrequent, absent or very irregular, excess facial or body hair, persistent acne, unexplained weight gain, or difficulty conceiving after a year of trying. Seek prompt assessment for signs of rapid virilisation, such as a deepening voice or hair growth that develops over a few months, which suggest a different cause. Heavy, prolonged bleeding with dizziness or faintness needs urgent care.

urinary-incontinence.name: Urinary incontinence
urinary-incontinence.definition: The involuntary leakage of urine, from an occasional dribble on coughing to a complete loss of bladder control, caused by weakness of the pelvic floor and urethral sphincter, an overactive bladder muscle, obstruction to the outflow of urine or damage to the nerves that control the bladder.
urinary-incontinence.overview: Continence depends on the bladder storing urine at low pressure while the urethral sphincter and the pelvic floor muscles keep the outlet closed, and on the brain and spinal cord timing relaxation of the outlet with contraction of the bladder wall (the detrusor). Incontinence follows when any part of this fails. Stress incontinence is leakage when coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting or exercising raises the pressure in the abdomen above what a weakened sphincter and pelvic floor can resist; it is the commonest type in women, typically after childbirth and the menopause, and it also follows prostate surgery in men. Trans women keep the prostate after vaginoplasty; leakage after gender-affirming genital surgery relates to the shortened, repositioned urethra and the pelvic floor rather than to removal of the prostate. Urgency incontinence is leakage with a sudden, compelling need to pass urine, usually with frequency and waking at night, caused by the detrusor contracting before the bladder is full (overactive bladder). Mixed incontinence combines the two. Overflow incontinence is the constant dribbling of a bladder that cannot empty, usually because of an enlarged prostate or nerve damage, and functional incontinence is leakage in someone whose bladder works but who cannot reach the toilet in time. Incontinence is common, affects women more often than men and becomes more frequent with age, but it is not a normal or inevitable part of ageing and most people can be helped.
causes: Weakness of the pelvic floor and urethral sphincter after pregnancy and vaginal birth, with the menopause, or after prostate surgery in men (stress incontinence)
Overactivity of the detrusor muscle, often without a clear cause, or from irritation of the bladder by infection, stones or a tumour (urgency incontinence)
Neurological disease that disrupts bladder control: stroke, Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury and nerve damage from diabetes
Obstruction to outflow from an enlarged prostate, a urethral stricture or a severe prolapse, leading to chronic retention with overflow
Medicines that increase urine output or affect bladder control, including diuretics such as furosemide, sedatives, some antidepressants, alpha-blockers and drugs with anticholinergic effects
Pelvic organ prolapse, pelvic surgery or radiotherapy, and rarely a fistula between the bladder and the vagina
Temporary causes such as urinary tract infection, constipation, or excess alcohol and caffeine
riskFactors: Pregnancy and vaginal childbirth, especially with a large baby or an instrumental delivery
Prostate enlargement or prostatectomy in men
Neurological conditions, diabetes, and limited mobility or cognitive impairment
signs: Leakage seen from the urethra when the person coughs with a comfortably full bladder
Weak pelvic floor muscle contraction, or pelvic organ prolapse, on vaginal examination
An enlarged prostate on rectal examination, or a painless distended bladder that can be felt in chronic retention
Vaginal atrophy after the menopause
Neurological signs such as leg weakness, altered sensation around the perineum or abnormal reflexes when a nerve cause is suspected
Sore, irritated skin in the groin and perineum from repeated wetting
complications: Skin irritation, rashes and pressure damage from persistent wetness
Recurrent urinary tract infections, particularly when the bladder does not empty fully
Falls and fractures in older adults hurrying to the toilet, especially at night
Disturbed sleep, embarrassment, social withdrawal, depression and reduced physical activity
Kidney damage from back-pressure in long-standing, untreated retention with overflow
Loss of independence; incontinence is a common reason for admission to a care home
urinary-incontinence.diagnosis: The history sorts the leakage into stress, urgency or mixed by asking when it happens, and covers fluid, caffeine and alcohol intake, medicines, bowel habit, childbirth, prostate symptoms and any neurological symptoms. A bladder diary kept for at least three days records the volumes drunk and passed, episodes of urgency and leakage, and night-time voids. Urinalysis excludes infection and blood, and a urine culture is sent if infection is suspected. Examination includes the abdomen for a distended bladder, a vaginal examination for prolapse, atrophy and pelvic floor strength, a rectal examination of the prostate in men, and a neurological check if the story suggests a nerve cause. A bladder scan after voiding measures the residual urine when emptying seems incomplete. NICE recommends urodynamic studies before surgery for stress incontinence when the diagnosis is uncertain or symptoms are mixed, and cystoscopy for blood in the urine, bladder pain or recurrent infection; blood in the urine, a pelvic mass, previous pelvic surgery or radiotherapy and suspected neurological disease are reasons for specialist referral.
urinary-incontinence.treatment: Treatment starts with conservative measures; NICE NG123 covers women and the same principles apply to men. Advice includes less caffeine, fluid intake that is neither excessive nor restricted, weight loss if overweight, stopping smoking and treating constipation. For stress incontinence a supervised programme of pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months is first line and is then continued as a habit; if it is not enough, the options are surgery (colposuspension, an autologous fascial sling or a mid-urethral sling, with mesh use restricted in the UK), urethral bulking injections, or duloxetine, which NICE does not recommend routinely. Vaginal oestrogen helps postmenopausal women with vaginal atrophy and urgency symptoms. For urgency incontinence and overactive bladder, bladder training for at least six weeks comes first, then an antimuscarinic or the beta-3 agonist mirabegron; for resistant symptoms, botulinum toxin injected into the bladder wall, which can leave the bladder unable to empty and so is offered only to people who are willing and able to learn clean intermittent self-catheterisation, or percutaneous tibial or sacral nerve stimulation in specialist services. Antimuscarinics commonly cause dry mouth and constipation and can affect memory and balance, so NICE advises avoiding immediate-release oxybutynin in frail older people; mirabegron needs blood pressure monitoring. Overflow incontinence is treated by relieving the cause, with intermittent self-catheterisation if the bladder cannot empty. Men with leakage after prostate surgery may be offered a male sling or an artificial sphincter, and pelvic floor physiotherapy is also used after gender-affirming genital surgery.
urinary-incontinence.prevention: Pelvic floor muscle training during and after pregnancy, and continued through life, reduces the risk of stress incontinence; NICE advises a supervised programme of pelvic floor muscle training in a first pregnancy as a preventive measure. Keeping to a healthy weight, not smoking, avoiding constipation, limiting caffeine and alcohol, and drinking neither far too much nor too little fluid all help. Treating a chronic cough, reviewing medicines that affect the bladder and good control of diabetes lower the risk, and men can learn pelvic floor exercises before prostate surgery.
urinary-incontinence.seekCare: See a GP about any leakage of urine that bothers you, however small; it is common, rarely mentioned and usually improvable, and a GP can refer to continence services or pelvic health physiotherapy. Seek urgent help for a sudden inability to pass urine with a painful, swollen lower abdomen (acute retention); for new incontinence with severe back pain, numbness around the buttocks or genitals, or weakness in the legs, which can mean compression of the nerves at the base of the spine and is an emergency; and for blood in the urine, pain on passing urine with fever, or sudden confusion in an older person, which may indicate infection.

angina.name: Angina
angina.definition: Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the heart muscle does not get enough blood.
angina.overview: Angina is chest discomfort caused by reduced blood flow to the heart. The NHS says it is usually due to coronary heart disease, where fatty deposits narrow the arteries that supply the heart. It is often brought on by physical effort or stress and tends to ease within a few minutes of rest. The British Heart Foundation describes four main types: stable, unstable, vasospastic and microvascular angina. The NHS describes angina as a warning sign of a risk of serious problems such as heart attacks and strokes.
causes: Narrowing of the arteries that supply the heart muscle, usually from a build-up of fatty deposits (coronary heart disease).
Spasm of a coronary artery, as in vasospastic angina.
riskFactors: High blood pressure or high cholesterol
signs: A GP may check blood pressure, BMI and cholesterol when angina is suspected.
An ECG records the heart's rhythm and electrical activity.
complications: Angina is a warning sign of a risk of serious problems such as heart attacks and strokes, according to the NHS.
Unstable angina carries a higher risk of a heart attack, according to the BHF.
angina.diagnosis: A GP may check blood pressure, BMI and cholesterol and ask about symptoms and family history. If angina is suspected, NHS 111 Wales says the person is referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist). Hospital tests listed by the NHS include an ECG, an exercise ECG, coronary angiography and blood tests.
angina.treatment: The NHS describes three main approaches: medicines to relieve attacks, medicines to prevent attacks, and surgery. For stable angina, the usual approach is a medicine used during an attack, glyceryl trinitrate (GTN), with other medicines to prevent attacks and reduce heart risk. Some people need surgery, such as angioplasty with a stent or a coronary artery bypass graft.
angina.prevention: The BHF lists stopping smoking, staying active and keeping weight, cholesterol, blood pressure and diabetes under control as central to managing angina. The NHS says avoiding triggers such as stress, cold weather and large meals can help prevent attacks.
angina.seekCare: Call 999 if chest pain does not ease after resting or after angina medicine, spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, or comes with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or breathlessness. For chest pain that goes away within a few minutes, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment. Someone with chest pain on exertion that eases with rest and no diagnosis is advised to contact the GP practice.

references.title: NHS: Common questions about glyceryl trinitrate (GTN)
British Heart Foundation: Angina common questions answered

sections.heading: What does angina feel like?
sections.body:
Chest pain could be angina if it feels tight, dull or heavy, spreads to the arms, neck, jaw or back, is triggered by physical effort or stress, and stops within a few minutes of rest, according to the NHS. Some people also have breathlessness, nausea or tiredness. Stable angina typically lasts five minutes or less.

Angina is often set off by physical effort or stress and tends to ease with rest or angina medicine. The NHS says avoiding triggers such as stress, cold temperatures and large meals can help prevent attacks. The BHF notes that angina is not a mini heart attack and generally does not leave lasting damage. A heart attack is different: its symptoms usually last longer and are not relieved by rest or by GTN spray.

Angina and heart attack symptoms can overlap. The BHF says angina-like symptoms that do not settle with rest or GTN could be the start of a heart attack, and the NHS advises calling 999 for an ambulance if symptoms do not stop within a few minutes.

sections.heading: What are the different types of angina?
sections.body:
The BHF describes four main types of angina. Stable angina is the most common. It is typically brought on by exertion and generally eases with rest or medicine. Unstable angina is less predictable. It can occur at rest, may not respond well to medicine, and carries a higher risk of a heart attack, according to the BHF.

Vasospastic angina, also called Prinzmetal's angina or variant angina, is caused by a coronary artery going into spasm. It usually comes on at rest, often in the early morning or at night, and people with it typically do not get angina during exercise.

Microvascular angina, also called cardiac syndrome X, affects the smallest coronary arteries and tends to appear under physical or emotional stress. The BHF notes that it can occur alongside vasospastic angina.

sections.heading: How is angina diagnosed?
sections.body:
According to the NHS, assessment starts with a GP, who asks about symptoms, lifestyle and family history. The GP measures blood pressure, calculates body mass index (BMI) from weight and height, measures waist size and takes blood to check cholesterol. NHS inform says the checks can include blood tests for diabetes or anaemia.

If a GP thinks someone may have angina, NHS 111 Wales says the person is referred to a heart specialist, called a cardiologist. Hospital tests listed by the NHS include an ECG, an exercise ECG, coronary angiography and blood tests. An ECG is a test that checks the heart's rhythm and electrical activity.

The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute notes that an ECG can help recognise types of angina and other serious heart problems, but the result may be normal even in someone who has angina. It also says tests can help rule out other conditions and show whether urgent medical attention is needed.

sections.heading: How is angina treated?
sections.body:
The NHS describes three main approaches: medicines to relieve attacks, medicines to prevent attacks, and surgery. Glyceryl trinitrate, known as GTN, is the usual medicine for an attack and comes as a mouth spray or tablets that dissolve under the tongue. The NHS says GTN works by widening blood vessels.

To prevent attacks, the NHS lists beta blockers, which slow the heart and reduce the force of its contraction, and calcium channel blockers, which widen the arteries. Low-dose aspirin, statins and ACE inhibitors are used to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke. NICE guidance for stable angina recommends offering either a beta blocker or a calcium channel blocker first, and says statin treatment is offered in line with its lipid guidance.

Some people need surgery. Coronary angioplasty with stenting widens a narrowed artery using a small tube called a stent. A coronary artery bypass graft reroutes blood around a blocked section using a vessel taken from elsewhere in the body. Common GTN side effects are headache, dizziness and facial flushing, and the NHS notes that stopping regular GTN may make angina worse.

sections.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
sections.body:
The NHS says to call 999 if chest pain does not stop after resting for a few minutes or after taking angina medicine. It also lists pain that spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, and chest pain with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or shortness of breath, as reasons to call 999. The NHS advises against driving oneself to A&E.

For chest pain that has not been diagnosed, the NHS advises stopping and resting, and calling 999 for an ambulance if symptoms do not stop within a few minutes. If the pain goes away within a few minutes, the NHS advises making an urgent GP appointment. Someone with chest pain on exertion that eases with rest and no diagnosis is advised to contact the GP practice.

Because angina and heart attack symptoms overlap, the NHS says that anyone who is unsure should call 999 for an ambulance.

faqs.q: Is angina the same as a heart attack?
faqs.a: No. The BHF says angina is not a mini heart attack and generally does not leave lasting damage. Angina usually eases within a few minutes of rest or GTN, while heart attack symptoms usually last longer and are not relieved by rest or GTN spray. Angina is also a signal of a greater risk of a heart attack, so the NHS advises calling 999 if symptoms do not stop within a few minutes.

faqs.q: Can angina be controlled?
faqs.a: The NHS says that with symptoms well controlled and healthy lifestyle changes, people can usually have a normal life with angina, and that with treatment symptoms should improve over time and may eventually stop. Treatment includes medicines to relieve and prevent attacks, and some people need surgery such as angioplasty or a bypass graft.

faqs.q: What does GTN do?
faqs.a: GTN (glyceryl trinitrate) is the usual medicine for an angina attack, according to the NHS. It comes as a mouth spray or tablets that dissolve under the tongue and works by widening blood vessels. The NHS lists headache, dizziness and facial flushing as common side effects, and notes that stopping regular GTN may make angina worse.

faqs.q: When should chest pain prompt a 999 call?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 if chest pain does not stop after resting for a few minutes or after angina medicine, spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, or comes with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or shortness of breath. For chest pain that goes away within a few minutes, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment. Anyone unsure whether symptoms are angina or a heart attack should call 999.

keyFacts.value: Narrowed arteries from a fatty build-up, as the NHS describes

diverticulitis.name: Diverticular disease and diverticulitis
diverticulitis.definition: Diverticular disease is a condition in which small pouches in the wall of the large intestine cause symptoms, and diverticulitis is when those pouches become inflamed or infected.
diverticulitis.overview: Diverticula are small pouches that bulge out of the wall of the large intestine. Pouches are common as people get older, and most people with them have no symptoms. When the pouches cause symptoms, doctors use the term diverticular disease. Diverticulitis, in which the pouches become inflamed or infected, most often causes abdominal pain, which is usually severe. Possible complications include an abscess, a blockage, a hole in the bowel, bleeding and fistulas.
causes: Small pouches form and bulge out of the wall of the large intestine.
Experts are not sure what causes diverticular disease and diverticulitis.
Diverticulitis happens when the pouches become inflamed or infected.
riskFactors: A diet low in fibre and high in red meat, which may be linked to higher risk
Genes may make some people more likely to develop the disease
signs: A high temperature
Blood in the stool
In severe illness, signs of sepsis such as confusion or pale, blotchy skin
complications: A fistula, an abnormal connection between the bowel and another organ such as the bladder
diverticulitis.diagnosis: Doctors review the person's history, carry out a physical examination and order tests. Doctors may order blood tests, a stool test, imaging tests (typically a CT scan) and a colonoscopy, which may be recommended to confirm a diagnosis and rule out other conditions such as cancer. NICE offers a full blood count and C-reactive protein test to people with suspected complicated diverticulitis who are referred for same-day hospital assessment.
diverticulitis.treatment: The NHS says a high-fibre diet can often ease symptoms of diverticular disease, and paracetamol can be used to relieve pain. Mild diverticulitis can usually be treated at home with antibiotics prescribed by a GP, and more serious cases may need hospital care, usually with intravenous antibiotics. Surgery to remove the affected section of bowel is sometimes recommended after serious complications, although this is rare.
diverticulitis.prevention: The NHS lists increasing fibre slowly, drinking plenty of water, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight among the things people can do. MedlinePlus says whether a low-fibre diet leads to this problem is not well proven.
diverticulitis.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, heavy bleeding from the bottom, or signs of sepsis such as confusion, pale or blotchy skin or fast breathing. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, tummy pain that is getting worse or not going away, a high temperature, or repeated vomiting that stops fluids staying down.

NICE: Diverticular disease: diagnosis and management (NG147), recommendations
Health Research Authority: The gut microbiome in diverticulitis and diverticulosis (research summary)

sections.heading: What is the difference between diverticulosis, diverticular disease and diverticulitis?
sections.body:
The word diverticula describes small pouches that form in the wall of the large intestine, which is also called the bowel. Having the pouches, known as diverticulosis, usually causes no discomfort, and most people with them never notice. Sometimes they are found by chance during tests done for another reason.

Diverticular disease is the term used when the pouches cause symptoms. It can cause constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or bloating. Diverticulitis is the stage in which the pouches become inflamed or infected, as the NHS describes it.

NIDDK, a United States institute, says experts are not sure what causes these conditions. It says research suggests that certain genes may make some people more likely to develop diverticular disease. NIDDK also says diverticulosis is quite common, especially as people age, and NHS inform says most people with pouches have no symptoms.

sections.heading: What does diverticulitis feel like?
sections.body:
Diverticulitis most often causes abdominal pain, which is usually severe. The NHS lists severe, constant tummy pain and a high temperature among the symptoms, alongside constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and blood in the stool. Diverticular disease can also cause constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or bloating.

Complications can include an abscess, a blockage, a hole in the bowel, bleeding and fistulas. NHS inform describes an abscess as a pus-filled cavity, and a fistula as an abnormal connection between the bowel and another organ such as the bladder.

NHS inform says surgery to remove the affected section of bowel is sometimes recommended after serious complications, although this is rare. Tummy pain that is getting worse or not going away, a high temperature, or blood in the stool are features for which the NHS advises getting urgent advice.

sections.heading: How do doctors diagnose diverticulitis?
sections.body:
Doctors start with the person's history and a physical examination. NIDDK says they may then order blood tests, a stool test, imaging tests and a colonoscopy. Imaging is typically a CT scan. A colonoscopy may be recommended to confirm a diagnosis of diverticular disease and to rule out other conditions, such as cancer.

NIDDK also says doctors ask about symptoms, bowel habits, what the person eats and drinks, medical conditions and medicines. Pouches are often found by chance during tests done for other reasons.

For people with suspected complicated acute diverticulitis who are referred for same-day hospital assessment, NICE guideline NG147 offers a full blood count, a urea and electrolytes test and a C-reactive protein test. The NICE committee called contrast CT the gold standard diagnostic test for acute diverticulitis and its complications.

sections.heading: How is diverticulitis treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on whether the problem is diverticular disease or diverticulitis and on how unwell the person is. The NHS says a high-fibre diet can often ease symptoms of diverticular disease, and paracetamol can be used to relieve pain.

For diverticulitis, the NHS says mild cases can usually be treated at home with antibiotics prescribed by a GP, while more serious cases may need hospital care, usually with intravenous antibiotics.

NICE guideline NG147 sets out different routes. People who are unwell all over the body but do not need referral are offered antibiotics by mouth. Those admitted to hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein. Where a CT scan confirms uncomplicated acute diverticulitis, NICE says the need for antibiotics is reviewed, taking account of other medical conditions.

NICE recommends against offering antibiotics or an aminosalicylate medicine to prevent diverticulitis from coming back.

sections.heading: Can diet and lifestyle make a difference?
sections.body:
The NHS self-care advice includes increasing fibre slowly, drinking plenty of water, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight. It also says NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen and opioids such as codeine can cause stomach problems or constipation and raise the risk of a bowel perforation.

MedlinePlus says providers may recommend a diet high in fibre and low in red meat, regular physical activity and not smoking. However, it also states that whether a low-fibre diet leads to the problem is not well proven.

Reviews on the NIH library site link low-fibre, high-red-meat diets, obesity, smoking, inactivity and regular NSAID use with higher risk. NIDDK says NSAIDs may increase the chance of diverticulitis complications.

Researchers are studying whether changes in gut bacteria and immune responses play a role, but a cause has not been established.

sections.heading: When should I get help for tummy pain or a high temperature?
sections.body:
The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, or being unable to pass stool or wind. The same applies to heavy bleeding from the bottom and to signs of sepsis, such as confusion, pale or blotchy skin, or fast breathing.

An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, tummy pain that is getting worse or not going away, a high temperature, or repeated vomiting that stops fluids staying down.

NHS inform lists reasons for hospital admission, including pain that paracetamol cannot control, being unable to drink enough fluids, being unable to take antibiotics by mouth, suspected complications, or no improvement after two days at home.

faqs.q: Is diverticulitis the same as diverticulosis?
faqs.a: No. Diverticulosis means having the small pouches in the wall of the large intestine, which usually causes no symptoms. Diverticular disease is the term used when the pouches cause symptoms or problems. Diverticulitis is when the pouches become inflamed or infected.

faqs.q: Does diverticulitis always need antibiotics?
faqs.a: NICE guideline NG147 offers antibiotics by mouth to people who are unwell all over the body but not referred to hospital. People in hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein. Where a CT scan confirms uncomplicated acute diverticulitis, NICE says the need for antibiotics is reviewed, taking account of other medical conditions.

faqs.q: Which painkillers does the NHS mention for diverticular disease?
faqs.a: The NHS lists painkillers such as paracetamol among the treatments for diverticular disease symptoms. It says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, and opioids such as codeine, can cause stomach problems or constipation and raise the risk of a bowel perforation. A GP can advise on the right choice for an individual.

faqs.q: Can diet prevent diverticular disease?
faqs.a: Experts are not sure what causes it, according to NIDDK. MedlinePlus lists diets low in fibre and high in red meat among lifestyle factors, and says providers may recommend a diet high in fibre and low in red meat. MedlinePlus also says it is not well proven that a low-fibre diet leads to the condition.

faqs.q: Is diverticulitis an emergency?
faqs.a: It can be. The NHS advises calling 999 for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, heavy bleeding from the bottom or signs of sepsis. For blood or mucus in the stool, worsening pain, a high temperature or repeated vomiting, it advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

keyFacts.label: Where it occurs
keyFacts.value: The large intestine (bowel)

keyFacts.label: The pouches
keyFacts.value: Small pouches called diverticula; common as people get older

keyFacts.label: Inflamed or infected pouches
keyFacts.value: This is diverticulitis

keyFacts.label: Main symptom
keyFacts.value: Abdominal pain, usually severe in diverticulitis

keyFacts.label: Tests that may be used
keyFacts.value: Blood tests, imaging (typically CT) and sometimes colonoscopy

keyFacts.label: Treatment
keyFacts.value: Pain relief, antibiotics for diverticulitis where needed, surgery only rarely

keyFacts.label: Emergency route
keyFacts.value: Call 999 for severe pain with vomiting or a swollen tummy

fatty-liver-disease.name: Fatty liver disease (MASLD)
fatty-liver-disease.definition: A common condition in which fat builds up in the liver, often linked to being overweight.
fatty-liver-disease.overview: Fatty liver disease linked to metabolic problems is now called MASLD and was formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). The NHS says it is a common condition that can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes. It does not usually cause symptoms and is often found when tests done for another reason show a problem with the liver. The British Liver Trust says that in some people it can progress to scarring, and in a small number to cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer.
causes: Fat builds up in the liver, often in people who are overweight.
Experts are still studying the causes; NIDDK names certain health problems and genes among possible contributors.
signs: Often none
Yellow skin and eyes (jaundice), itchy skin, or swelling of the legs, ankles, feet or tummy, when cirrhosis has developed
complications: Inflammation of the liver (MASH, formerly NASH)
Liver failure and liver cancer in a small number of people
fatty-liver-disease.diagnosis: The NHS says fatty liver disease can be diagnosed using blood tests and sometimes an ultrasound scan of the tummy. An NHS trust page says a GP may order further blood tests, and sometimes an ultrasound scan, to confirm fat in the liver, rule out other causes and check for liver damage. NIDDK says doctors may use blood tests, imaging tests and a liver biopsy to diagnose the disease and to tell simple fatty liver from the inflamed form. NICE recommends that people with the condition are offered testing for advanced liver fibrosis. It also says the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test can be considered.
fatty-liver-disease.treatment: The NHS describes healthy lifestyle change as the core treatment. When there is scarring of the liver, the NHS says a liver specialist may prescribe pioglitazone or vitamin E.
fatty-liver-disease.prevention: The British Liver Trust says eating healthily, being physically active and staying at a healthy weight reduce the amount of fat in the liver. The NHS also advises not smoking.
fatty-liver-disease.seekCare: The NHS says a person with diagnosed cirrhosis who has yellow skin or eyes, or swelling in the tummy, legs, ankles or feet, should ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomiting blood, very dark or black tarry stools, or periods of confusion or drowsiness. MedlinePlus advises seeing a health care provider for unusual symptoms such as fatigue or abdominal pain.

sections.heading: What is fatty liver disease?
sections.body:
Fatty liver disease means fat has built up in the liver. The NHS describes it as a common condition that is often linked to being overweight and can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes. It was long called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD. The British Liver Trust says metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD, will replace that name, and that some pages still use the older one.

The British Liver Trust describes MASH as the more serious form. MedlinePlus says NASH is now called MASH. NIDDK distinguishes simple fatty liver from the inflamed form, NASH, and describes both as part of the same disease. The British Liver Trust says that in some people MASLD can progress to liver scarring, called fibrosis. It says that in a small number of people it can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer. NIDDK notes that experts are still studying the causes, and names certain health problems and genes among possible contributors.

sections.heading: Does fatty liver disease cause symptoms?
sections.body:
The NHS says fatty liver disease does not usually cause any symptoms. NIDDK calls NAFLD and NASH most often silent diseases with few or no symptoms. An NHS trust page says the condition is often found when blood tests or scans done for another reason show a problem with the liver.

Some people do have symptoms. The NHS lists feeling very tired, feeling generally unwell, and pain or discomfort under the right side of the ribs. MedlinePlus lists fatigue and pain in the upper right abdomen as the most common symptoms when they do appear.

NHS 111 Wales describes jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), itchy skin and swelling of the legs, ankles, feet or tummy as symptoms of cirrhosis, the most advanced stage. NIDDK warns, on its page for children, that once symptoms arise a child may already have permanent liver damage.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says fatty liver disease can be diagnosed using blood tests and sometimes an ultrasound scan of the tummy. An NHS trust page says a GP may order further blood tests, and sometimes an ultrasound scan, to confirm fat in the liver, to rule out other causes and to check for liver damage. NIDDK says doctors may use blood tests, imaging tests and a liver biopsy to diagnose the disease and to tell simple fatty liver from the inflamed form.

Fibrosis means scarring of the liver. NICE recommends that people with the condition are offered testing for advanced liver fibrosis. It also says the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test can be considered, and it advises against using routine liver blood tests on their own to assess for advanced fibrosis. NICE advises that adults and young people diagnosed with advanced fibrosis are referred to a specialist in hepatology, the branch of medicine that deals with the liver.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease treated?
sections.body:
The NHS describes healthy lifestyle change as the core treatment. It advises a healthy balanced diet, regular exercise, weight loss for people who are overweight, limiting alcohol and not smoking. The British Liver Trust says losing weight and eating a healthy diet is the first line of treatment. It says eating healthily, being physically active and staying at a healthy weight reduce the amount of fat in the liver, which can slow down, stop and even reverse MASLD and MASH. NIDDK names weight loss as the main recommendation.

An NHS trust page says that without liver damage, lifestyle changes are generally the only treatment needed. When there is scarring of the liver, the NHS says a liver specialist may prescribe pioglitazone or vitamin E. MedlinePlus, a US source, describes a medicine called resmetirom, used with diet and exercise, for adults with NASH without cirrhosis who have moderate to advanced scarring.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease linked to type 2 diabetes?
sections.body:
The NHS lists type 2 diabetes among the factors linked to fatty liver disease, together with polycystic ovary syndrome and being over 50. It says the risk is higher in people who are overweight or have an unhealthy diet.

NIDDK says that in people with NAFLD, type 2 diabetes and being overweight or having obesity are key risk factors for simple fatty liver progressing to NASH and fibrosis. A review reports that diabetes promotes progression from simple fatty liver to NASH and increases the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.

The British Liver Trust says that in some people fatty liver disease progresses to scarring, and in a small number to cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer.

sections.heading: When should a person get help?
sections.body:
The NHS says a person with diagnosed cirrhosis who has yellow skin or eyes, or swelling in the tummy, legs, ankles or feet, should ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111. NHS 111 Wales gives similar advice for people with fatty liver disease and a liver condition who have jaundice, itchy skin or swelling.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomiting blood, very dark or black tarry stools, or periods of confusion or drowsiness, particularly when cirrhosis has been diagnosed.

MedlinePlus advises seeing a health care provider for unusual symptoms such as fatigue or abdominal pain.

faqs.q: Can fatty liver disease be reversed?
faqs.a: The NHS says fatty liver disease can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes. The British Liver Trust says eating healthily, being active and staying at a healthy weight reduce liver fat, which can slow down, stop and even reverse MASLD and MASH. NIDDK says weight loss can reduce liver fat, inflammation and scarring. When there is fibrosis or cirrhosis, a liver specialist may be involved.

faqs.q: Is MASLD the same as NAFLD?
faqs.a: MASLD is the newer name for what was called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD. The British Liver Trust says MASLD will replace the older name and that some pages still use it. The more serious inflamed form, MASH, was previously called NASH, and MedlinePlus says NASH is now called MASH.

faqs.q: Who is more likely to get fatty liver disease?
faqs.a: The NHS lists type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome and being over 50, and says the risk is higher in people who are overweight or have an unhealthy diet. NIDDK says type 2 diabetes and being overweight or having obesity are key risk factors for progression to NASH and fibrosis. Its children's page adds that genes may also play a part.

faqs.q: What tests are used to look for it?
faqs.a: The NHS says blood tests and sometimes an ultrasound scan of the tummy can be used. NIDDK says doctors may also use other imaging tests and a liver biopsy. NICE recommends that people with the condition are offered testing for advanced liver fibrosis, and says the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test can be considered.

keyFacts.label: Also called
keyFacts.value: NAFLD (non-alcoholic fatty liver disease); the inflamed form, MASH, was formerly NASH

keyFacts.label: Usual symptoms
keyFacts.value: Often none; some people feel tired or have discomfort under the right ribs

keyFacts.label: Often found
keyFacts.value: By blood tests or scans done for another reason

keyFacts.label: Main treatment
keyFacts.value: Healthy lifestyle change, including weight loss for people who are overweight

keyFacts.label: Linked conditions
keyFacts.value: Type 2 diabetes and polycystic ovary syndrome, according to the NHS; being overweight raises the risk

keyFacts.label: Possible progression
keyFacts.value: In some people scarring, and in a small number cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer (British Liver Trust)

keyFacts.label: Urgent signs
keyFacts.value: Yellow skin or eyes, or swelling of the tummy or legs, with cirrhosis: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111; vomiting blood: call 999

influenza.name: Flu (influenza)
influenza.definition: Flu is a respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses.
influenza.overview: Flu is an infection caused by influenza viruses. It comes on very quickly, with a sudden high temperature, aching body, tiredness, dry cough, sore throat and headache. Most people have a mild illness, but flu can lead to complications such as bronchitis and pneumonia, and older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with long-term conditions are at higher risk. The NHS says having the vaccine before the flu season starts is the best way to avoid catching and spreading flu.
causes: Infection with influenza viruses; types A and B cause the seasonal epidemics seen in people.
The virus spreads mainly in droplets made when people with flu cough, sneeze or talk.
The WHO says the virus can also be spread by hands contaminated with influenza viruses.
NHS inform says germs from coughs and sneezes can survive on hands and surfaces for 24 hours.
riskFactors: Long-term conditions such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease
signs: A sudden high temperature, aching body and dry cough
complications: Inflammation of the heart or brain
Worsening of long-term conditions such as asthma and heart disease
In some cases, treatment in hospital
influenza.diagnosis: Flu can be confirmed with a test on a swab from the nose or throat. MedlinePlus describes rapid antigen tests as the most common flu tests but says they are not as accurate as other types. It describes molecular laboratory tests as the most accurate type of flu test.
influenza.treatment: Most people recover at home with rest, plenty of fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen to lower a temperature and ease aches. GPs do not recommend antibiotics for flu, because it is caused by viruses. Antiviral medicines are prescription-only; the CDC recommends prompt treatment for people at higher risk of complications and says they work best when started within about two days. The NHS says aspirin should not be given to children under 16.
influenza.prevention: The NHS says having the vaccine before the flu season starts is the best way to avoid catching and spreading flu. NHS advice also includes washing hands often with warm water and soap, binning used tissues quickly, and covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing.
influenza.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, difficulty breathing or coughing up a lot of blood. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised when someone with flu symptoms is 65 or over, pregnant, has a long-term condition or a weakened immune system, or has not improved after 7 days. The CDC says most people with flu have a mild illness and do not need medical care.
